blocks.text: Invocation
Invocation
We worship [the flute], a second Rādhā: her body pressed by the leaf-like fingers of Govinda's tender hands, she increases rasa, and because her inner being is pure she is seated on [his] lips.
blocks.verse:
गोविन्द करपल्लव पत्रिका भिर्निष्पीडितांगीम् रस वर्धिनीम् वै ।
पूतात्मतत्वादधरोपविष्टाम् राधाम् द्वितीयामनुराधयाम् ।।१।।

blocks.text: The flute which, struck again and again by the leaves, that is the fingers, of Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa's tender-shoot hands, became rasa-vardhinī (one who increases rasa, aesthetic flavour); and which, being hollow like a soul free of deceit and guile, came to be seated on the Lord's adhara (lips), as if it were Śrī Kṛṣṇa's second Rādhā: such a flute we worship again and again.
Praise

Among instruments the flute, among scriptures the Gītā, among rivers the Gaṅgā, among cities Kāśī, among yogas devotion, and among people the mother: these always stand out for being both beneficial and dear.
blocks.verse:
वाद्येषु बंशी निगमेषु गीता नदीषु गंगा नगरेषु काशी।
योगेषु भक्तिश्च जनेषु माता हितप्रियाभ्याम् सततं विशिष्टाः।।२।।

blocks.text: In the world there are only a few things or persons that are dear as well as beneficial. For example: among instruments the flute, which purifies the prāṇa (breath) and sounds sweet to the ears; among scriptures the Gītā, which purifies the mind through yoga and is dear for its simplicity; among rivers the Gaṅgā, which delivers [us] from many diseases and gives creatures sweet and cool water; among cities Kāśī, which frees [us] from many kinds of sin and charms the mind with its beauty; among yogas bhakti (devotion), supremely dear, which removes the darkness of ignorance and lights the lamp of knowledge; and among people the mother, who wishes [our] good and speaks kindly. All these hold a special place in the world.
Just as the Gītā of Kṛṣṇa, lord of yoga, is dear to people, so the Kṛṣṇā flute is dear to those who have faith in music.
blocks.verse:
योगेश्वरस्य कृष्णस्य यथा गीता जनप्रिया।
संगीते श्रद्दधानानाम् कृष्णावंशी तथा प्रिया।।३।।

blocks.text: Just as the Gītā of Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa is dear to people, in the same way the āḍī bansī (transverse, side-blown flute) is very dear to lovers of music. If he recited the Gītā to free Arjuna from delusion, he played the flute to free the gopīs from attachment.
Therefore
Thinking 'may I too have devotion to Kṛṣṇa', I worship the flute; and practice of this instrument bestows the fruits beginning with dharma and artha (the four aims of life).
blocks.verse:
ममापि कृष्णे भक्तिः स्यादिति वंशीम् भजाम्यहम्।
साधना चास्य वाद्यस्य धर्मार्थादि फलप्रदा।।४।।

blocks.text: Thinking 'may I too have bhakti (devotion) for Śrī Kṛṣṇa', I worship the flute, because through its sādhanā (practice) the four fruits, dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa, are obtained.
Among instruments I consider the flute, with its fine seven notes, the most pleasing: because of its sweetness, because it costs little, because it is light, and because it can be had everywhere.
blocks.verse:
वाद्येषु रुचिरं मन्ये बंशीवाद्यं सुसप्तकम्।
माधुर्यादल्प मूल्यत्वा ल्लघुत्वात् सर्वसंभवात्।।५।।

blocks.text: Since this instrument is within easy reach of the poor and the rich alike, and can be found anywhere from the forest to the market, who would not love this simple and sweet instrument?
Part One: Making the Flute
Here Begins the Section on Making
The Origin of the Flute
Although learned men hold many views about its origin, in this scientific age my view is different from all of them, and reasoned.
When a piece of bamboo in the forest is sounded by the wind of its own accord, that single-note, self-born flute is made by the gods.
blocks.verse:
स्वेच्छया वायुनाऽरण्ये बंशखण्डो निनाद्यते।
एक स्वरा स्वयं भूता बंशी सा देवनिर्मिता।।६।।

blocks.text: That is

That is: from whenever half-cut bamboos in the forest began to sound by themselves through the impact of the wind, from then the origin of the ekasvarā (single-note) flute should be reckoned, which we can call devanirmitā (god-made).
Lord Kṛṣṇa, taking human form and wishing to play, himself devised the seven notes in the bamboo.
blocks.verse:
नररूपधरो भगवान् कृष्णः क्रीड़ां चिकीर्षयन्।
स्वराणाम् कल्पने वंशे सप्तानां कृत्वान् स्वयम्।।७।।

blocks.text: That is

In the same way, bamboos broken by the impact of the wind went on sounding for a long time, and they still do. Among them, broken bamboos of different lengths and widths have sometimes produced several nādas (musical sounds) at once. Curious forest-dwellers imitated them and began to play by blowing with the mouth. Then they made holes in it as they wished, and made it an instrument for folk songs. In the Vedas the name of the sage Tumburu comes up in connection with playing the flute.

Later, in the Dvāpara age, Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra gave the flute a special place in his childhood play and refined it further; he established the seven notes according to the śāstra, and used to play rāgas and rāginīs on it with skill.

Before this the flute had no separate mukharandhra (mouth-hole). Blowing from the natural opening alone, [players] drew three notes, which are described in the Vedas under the names udātta (raised accent), anudātta (lowered accent) and svarita (falling accent).
But when another age came, some master of song, because people wanted ease, made the Jihvāvatī (fipple flute).
blocks.verse:
युगान्तरे तु संप्राप्ते मानवैर्लाधवेच्छया।
बंशीम् जिह्वावतीम् चक्रे कश्चिद् गीतविशारदः।।८।।

blocks.text: That is

Then, in the Kali age, some convenience-seeking scientific musician made a jibbhī (fipple) in it, which made it still easier. Even children began to play it. But science holds development in one hand and destruction in the other. So the sweetness that comes into the sound on the āḍī bansī (transverse flute) through practice of the lips is, on the flute with a fipple, limited and dependent, and to some extent even harmful to health. Because it is so easy, it sometimes gets broken in children's hands.

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: The Three Kinds of Flute

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: Hence the flute is seen in the world in three kinds, resting on the three guṇas; their names are Tripurā, Kṛṣṇā and Jihvāvatī.
blocks.verse:
तेन बंशी तृधा लोके दृश्यते तृगुणात्मिका।
तासाम् नामानि त्रिपुराथ कृष्णा च जिह्वावती।।९।।

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: Thus three kinds of flute, the gift of three ages and based on the three guṇas, are mainly in use today. Their names are Tripurā (the flute blown from the bamboo's natural opening), Kṛṣṇā (the transverse, side-blown flute) and Jihvāvatī (the fipple flute). Then, on the basis of these, many suṣira vādya (wind instruments), such as the bīn (reed pipe) and the shehnai, are held to have arisen.

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: The method of making them that is approved by the science of sound (nāda-śāstra) is written here in essence, after reflection, with [my] small understanding.
blocks.verse:
निर्माणे या विधिस्तासाम् नादशास्त्रेण सम्मता।
लिख्यते साररूपेण लघुबुद्धया विविच्य च।।१०।।

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: The method of making them that accords with the śāstra I am writing down after reflecting on it with my small understanding. Perhaps this process of making will be useful to our flute-playing brothers.

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: As the inspiration of Kṛṣṇa, lord of yoga, may be, so is the understanding of people like me on the path of action.
blocks.verse:
योगेश्वरस्य कृष्णस्य प्रेरणा यादृशी भवेत।
मादृशाम् तादृशी बुद्धिर्जनानाम् कर्मवर्त्मनि।।११।।

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: I have no importance in writing this work, because the Lord's inspiration, working through circumstances, gets done by each person whatever work it wants done by them. So first of all I have to consider which metal is how useful for the flute.

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: Materials Suitable for a Flute

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: Copper is better than a piece of iron, and a piece of silver better than that; better than that is wood, and best of all is a piece of bamboo.
blocks.verse:
लौहखण्डात् तु ताम्रम् स्यात् तस्माद्रजत खण्डकम्।
तस्माच्छ्रेष्ठं तु काष्ठं स्यात् सर्वस्माद् बंश खण्डकम्।।१२।।

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: In the flute, nādotpatti (the production of sound) comes from the vibration of air, whatever solid casing that air may be enclosed in; even so, with different vessels there is always a subtle difference in the impact of the air. Among metals that conduct electricity, silver [and] aluminium are better than iron [and] copper, because it is good if the instrument is light. And non-conducting materials such as wood are said to be better than these. But bamboo, which produces supporting sounds through its aṇurandhra (micro-pores), is the best of all.

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: When the bamboo is well seasoned, the flute made from it excels, because self-born sounds arise in its micro-pores.
blocks.verse:
यदा बशं सुपक्वं स्यात् तस्य बंशी विशिष्यते।
अणु रन्ध्रेषु नादानाम् स्वयंभूनां च सम्भवात्।।१३।।

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: As far as the question of a suitable material for the flute goes, bamboo is the best. But even among bamboos, the better one is the bamboo that has matured (supakva, well seasoned) thoroughly and naturally. For in ripe bamboo, compared with green bamboo, the aṇurandhra (micro-pores), that is the fine fibres, become more distinct, and its capacity for supporting sound is also greater. Now the question is of making the flute.

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: Today, among flute players, those artists who do not know how to make a flute are unhappy. The problem before them is whom to have a flute made by, one that is true in tune and matches the desired pitch. If I have to play together in some ensemble, all the instruments will have one fixed pitch, and if my flute does not match it, then I shall have to seek the help of a skilled nirmātā (maker) who can make a flute as I want it. This problem can be fully solved only when artists make their own flutes. So now I shall set out the proper rules for making a flute, which by the grace of [my] guru I found after searching for years.

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: By the measure of the inner circumference, a length from the mouth-hole of more than six times and less than nine [times] has been well tested.
blocks.verse:
अन्तः परिधिमानेन मुखरात् षड्गुणाधिकम्।
नवतो न्यूनमित्येव मायतिः सुपरीक्षिता।।१४।।

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: First of all I have to fix the parimāṇa (measure) of the length of the bamboo or pipe, which is to be related to its width. So now I am going to do just that, because every person is three and a half hāth (hastas, cubits) tall by his own hand. This is easier with a pipe, because its width is the same throughout; a bamboo is wider at one end. So the width of the bamboo that counts will be the greater one.

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: So, to measure that width from inside, roll a piece of thick paper like a chhallā (ring) and put it into the pipe, and see that inside it fits the roundness of the pipe exactly and that the two edges of the paper meet; then take it out. As soon as it comes out, the paper will open out into a length, and just this will be taken as the inner width of the pipe (antaḥ paridhimāna, measure of the inner circumference), because I have to find the width of the body of air inside the pipe. Now let the length of the pipe be measured with the length of that paper: if it is from nine times to eight times, [it is] best; from eight to seven times, middling; and from seven to six times, poor. If it is less than even six times, it will not make a flute. Now, what objection can there be if the length is less or more than this regular measure? For that, attend to the following śloka -

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: If the piece of bamboo is made longer or shorter than that, then, in proportion to the breath, the lower and upper registers fall out of order.
blocks.verse:
ततोऽधिके च न्यूने च बंश खंडे प्रकल्पिते।
स्वासमानानुरोधेन मन्द्रतार व्यतिक्रमः।।१५।।

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: For a flute it is necessary that a note one saptaka (octave) higher than the note that sounds when the phūṅk (breath) is kept weak will sound when the breath is made strong. And for this one-octave difference to come out exactly on all seven notes, it is possible only if the length of the pipe or bamboo follows the rule given above, not otherwise. To test this I have blown and tried pieces of pipe from the smallest, whose length equalled the antaḥparidhimāna (measure of the inner circumference), up to the largest, which were 16 times that measure. The corrected measure that came out of this was then fixed. In any case, these days it is a problem for most flute players where to buy a tuneful flute. If someone has somehow trained his breath on an out-of-tune flute, then even another, tuneful flute will be out of tune for him.

blocks.subsection_title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
blocks.text: Now it must be made clear here how the proper length stated for the flute is valid. If you measure the antaḥparidhi (inner circumference), that is the inner girth, of a pipe and cut the pipe to just that length, then the length and width of the air inside it, which has to be set in motion by the breath, will become equal, and it cannot be set in motion by the breath; so only a bare sound (nāda) will arise in it. If its length is made four times, two sounds can be produced by the breath, about an octave apart. Now if a hole is made in the pipe at 5 times the length, two sounds exactly an octave apart can be produced. So it must be accepted that if we need two forms of each of the seven notes, one octave apart from each other by just lessening or increasing the breath, then for this a pipe of eight times will be right. For if one makes a mukharandhra (mouth-hole) in a pipe of eight times and blows, then as the vega (force) of the breath is raised step by step, 4 sounds of this kind are seen to arise: Sa Ṡa Ṗa Ṡa. With skilful blowing one more sound will come, which we can call the G̈a of the ati-tāra saptaka (very high octave). This is the meaning of the following śloka.
Placing the Notes
That bamboo in which, by varying the blowing, five notes arise in order, Sa, Sa, Pa, Sa, Ga, is the one approved by the śāstra of the flute.
blocks.verse:
यत्र फूत्कार भंदेन क्रमात् पंचस्वरोदयः।
सस प सा ग इत्येव स वंश शास्त्र संमतः।।१६।।

blocks.text: So if I have to make a flute, I shall need a pipe or bamboo long enough to be about ten times its antaḥparidhi (inner circumference). In it, at the first dasāṃśa (one-tenth) from one end, that is 10/1, make the hole of the mukharandhra (mouth-hole).

The roundness of the mukharandhra (mouth-hole) will be 1/3, that is one-third, of the antarvyāsa (inner diameter). From the other end too, at a distance of the first dasāṃśa (one-tenth), that is 10/1, make a hole whose inner diameter is half, that is 1/2, of the paridhimāna (measure of the circumference). So the length left from the mouth-hole to that second hole is 8 times, by the paridhimāna. And taking as Sa the nāda (sound) that arises when blowing into the mouth-hole, place the further notes in the following way -
Now, before [placing] the six notes, one must find a place where, by making a hole, a note exactly one saptaka (octave) higher, that is (Ṡa), can sound. On this there is the following śloka.
By the measure of the inner circumference, at four times [that measure] from the mouth-hole lies the upper Ṣaḍja, if the middle [Ṣaḍja] lies at the tenth.
blocks.verse:
अन्तः परिधि मानेन मुख रन्ध्रा च्चतुर्गुणे।
परिमाणे षडजस्तारों यदि मध्यो दशमे स्थितः।।१७।।

blocks.text: The meaning of the above śloka is that the length from the mukharandhra (mouth-hole) to the far end of the pipe, measured by the paridhimāna (measure of the circumference) given before, may be as much as nine times and as little as six times.

Now, whatever the length from the mouth-hole to the end, the sound that comes out when it is blown is named (madhya Sa, middle Sa). Now divide the distance from madhya Sa to the mouth-hole into ten equal parts, and at 4/10 part from the mouth-hole, that is at 6/10 part from madhya Sa, make a mark with a pencil; its name will be tāra Ṡa (upper Sa). After this, between these two Sas, 11 more marks will have to be made in the way given below; then in all 11+2=13 notes will have been placed, whose names will be: Sa, komal Re, Re, komal Ga, Ga, Ma, Ma′, Pa, komal Dha, Dha, komal Ni, Ni, Ṡa.
Between the two Ṣaḍjas the Madhyama note is wanted; between Ṣaḍja and Madhyama the wise should place Ṛṣabha.
blocks.verse:
षडजद्वय मध्ये तु मध्यमः स्वर इष्यते।
षडज मध्यमयो र्मध्ये रिषभः स्थाप्यो मनीषिभीः।।१८।।

blocks.text: That is, between the two Sas make the mark for the śuddha (natural) Madhyama note, and between that Madhyama and madhya Sa place śuddha Ṛṣabha.

Here the derivation of Ṣaḍja fits as follows: the note that ṣaṭ svarān, that is six notes, janayati, that is gives birth to, is called Ṣaḍja; and the note that stands in the middle of the saptaka (octave) is called Madhyama. In short these are called Sa and Ma, and Ṛṣabha is called Re.
Between Ṛṣabha and Madhyama two Gāndhāras are to be devised; between the other Ṣaḍja and Madhyama, komal Dhaivata.
blocks.verse:
रिषभमध्यमयोर्मध्ये गान्धारद्वय कल्पना।
अपरषडज् मध्यमयोर्मध्ये कोमल धैवतः।।१९।।

blocks.text: That is, between the Ṛṣabha and Madhyama notes make the marks for two Gāndhāras at equal distance. And between tāra Sa and the Madhyama note make the mark for komal Dhaivata.
Between ṛju Dhaivata and Madhyama two notes are to be placed in order: the first will be tīvra Madhyama, the second Pañcama.
blocks.verse:
ऋजुधैवत मध्यमयोर्मध्ये स्थाप्यौस्वरौ क्रमात्।
प्रथमो मध्यमस्तीब्रो द्वितीयः पंचमोभवेत।।२०।।

blocks.text: That is, between komal Dhaivata and Madhyama understand the places of two notes at equal distance: the first will be tīvra (sharp) Madhyama and the second the Pañcama note.
Between ṛju Dhaivata and Ṣaḍja three parts are held: the first is śuddha Dhaivata, the second [and third] the two Niṣādas.
blocks.verse:
ऋजुधैवत षड्जयोर्मध्ये भागास्त्रयो मताः।
प्रथमो धैवतः शुद्धो द्वितीयौ द्वौ निषादकौ।।२१।।

blocks.text: That is, between komal Dhaivata and tāra Ṣaḍja the wise should make three equal parts and place, in order, Dhaivata and the two Niṣādas.
Between Ṛṣabha and Ṣaḍja is komal Ṛṣabha. Thus one should devise these twelve svarasthānas (note positions).
blocks.verse:
ऋषभषड्जयोमध्ये कोमलो ऋषभो भवेत्।
स्वरस्थानानि चैतानि द्वादशानि प्रकल्पयेत्।।२२।।

blocks.text: That is, between Ṛṣabha and madhya Sa is the place of komal Ṛṣabha. In this way place all twelve notes in the form of marks.

An example is given here on the basis of the rule above. Suppose we printed the roundness of a pipe or bamboo on paper and found its roundness to be about 6 sūt [a small unit of length]. Then I measured the inner girth of that roundness, opened it out and measured it: the paper that sat inside in the shape of a round ring of 6 sūt became, after opening out, about 17 sūt long, that is 1 inch 7 sūt. Now we named this paper (antaḥparidhimāna, measure of the inner circumference), and gave it a short name too, miti (the measure). Then we cut a pipe 7 times as long as this miti and found it came to about 12 inches. When a mukharandhra (mouth-hole) was made at one end, the pipe from the mouth-hole to the end was some ten and a half inches long. Now, first of all, in order to place tāra Ṣaḍja, a mark was made at a distance of four inches two sūt down from the mouth-hole and taken as tāra Ṡa. And the far end of the pipe was taken as madhya Sa, since it is between these two Sas that we have to place the 12 notes. If the space between the two Sas were divided into 6 equal parts and Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni placed in order, the flute would certainly be out of tune. For as we go on making holes moving upward, its area keeps decreasing, and in the same proportion the distance between the notes (svarāntara, interval) also keeps decreasing. It is with this fine point in mind that the rule above had to be made the basis. So in the figure the marks will not be at equal distances from bottom to top.

But after the marks are made, the holes on those marks must be made in order. By the rule above, madhya Ṣaḍja should not be taken to be the cut end of the pipe that stands naturally open. So, measuring with the miti (the measure of the inner circumference), a hole should be made at a distance of six miti from the mouth-hole, its girth about half the girth of the pipe; and about one miti below that hole should be the far end of the pipe. If a flute 7 times the miti is to be made, make the madhya Sa hole at the distance of 7 times. And if a flute longer than 7 times is to be made, place madhya Sa at that same distance too. But do not place the remaining notes by the rule above; for that we shall give some additional rules later. The rule above is only for those flutes that are 6 or 7 times their miti long. See the figure ahead.

Here, the place where the author has taken Ṣaḍja to be is, in the view of players, the place of the Pañcama note. Still, for the convenience of beginning sādhakas (learners), the Ṣaḍja given above is accepted. If, out of habit, the first hole on the flute, which is the lowest, is taken to be Pañcama rather than Ṣaḍja, then for them another method of placing the notes is set out. Although there is no special difference between this method and the one above, it is written to remove some people's doubts.
By the measure of the inner circumference, at four times from the mouth-hole lies the middle Pañcama, if the lower one lies at the tenth.
blocks.verse:
अन्तः परिधि मानेन मुखरन्ध्राच्चतुगुणे।
परिमाणे पंचमोमध्यो यदि मन्द्रो दशमे स्थितः।।२३।।

blocks.text: That is, if the other end of the pipe is at ten times from the mukharandhra (mouth-hole), then, taking that as mandra (lower) Pañcama, the Pañcama of the madhya saptaka (middle octave) must be taken at four times the distance from the mouth-hole. That is, if Pañcama is ten inches from the mouth-hole, place the second Pañcama four inches from the mouth-hole. Here it is not necessary that the length of the pipe be exactly ten times the paridhimāna (measure of the circumference). The length of the pipe can also be 7 or 8 times the paridhimāna; but we have to place madhya Pañcama by dividing that length into five equal parts and taking 2/5, or into ten parts and taking 4/10, because the remaining notes have to be placed taking just these two Pañcamas as pillars. If the far end of the pipe is not natural but artificial, that is if a hole is made and taken as the end, then in this case madhya Pañcama can be placed not at 4/10 but at 5/12. See the figure.
Between the two Pañcamas lies Ṣaḍja; between lower Pañcama and Ṣaḍja, Dhaivata is wanted.
blocks.verse:
पंचमद्वय मध्ये तु षडजस्य स्थिति र्भवेत।
मन्द्र पंचम षडजयो र्मध्ये धैवत इष्यते।।२४।।

blocks.text: That is, Ṣaḍja lies in the middle between the lower Pañcama and the upper Pañcama, and Dhaivata belongs midway between the lower Pañcama and Ṣaḍja. Here some inquirers may ask: since the distance from Dhaivata to Pañcama, counting komal Dhaivata, is two svarāntaras (intervals), and the distance from Dhaivata to Ṣaḍja, because of the two Niṣādas in between, is three intervals, why then has Dhaivata been placed midway between Ṣaḍja and Pañcama? This doubt is resolved as follows: once the hole of the Dhaivata note is made, the length of the pipe is reduced, and the result of this shortening is that within the same distance in which two notes lie below Dha, three notes can be placed above. Here a spiritual thought too will hold good: if a poor man loses ten paise and a rich man loses 10 rupees, both will feel equal distress. In the same way, in the pipe too the successive limits are seen to grow smaller: though to the ear the intervals between notes are equal, to the eye, as on a stringed instrument, the distance appears to shrink. On this basis, further on, four notes are placed within this same distance.
Between lower Pañcama and Dhaivata is komal Dhaivata; between Ṣaḍja and Dhaivata are the two Niṣādas, equally spaced.
blocks.verse:
मन्द्र पंचम धैवतयो र्मध्ये कोमल धैवतः।
षड्ज धैवतयो र्मध्ये निषादौ द्वौ समानकौ।।२५।।

blocks.text: That is, komal Dhaivata will be between the lower Pañcama and śuddha Dhaivata, and both Niṣādas will lie at equal distances between śuddha Dhaivata and Ṣaḍja. Here some may doubt: when, by the earlier rule, the gaps between the holes also contract as the pipe gets shorter, how is it that equal distances have been written for Dha, Ni, Ni and Sa? This will be resolved by the following śloka.
When a hole is narrowed, the sound becomes lower; when a hole is widened, the reverse.
blocks.verse:
यदा छिद्रस्य संकोचः स्थात्तदा नादनीचता।
यदा छिद्रस्य विस्तारस्तदा स्याद् विपरीतता।।२६।।

blocks.text: That is, in the distances between the holes of Dha, Ni, Ni and Sa there is so fine an unevenness that it is hard to solve by gaṇita (calculation). So the fault can be removed simply by making the komal Ni hole slightly smaller than the Dha hole. The proof of this can only be the attentive ear of musicians. So the meaning of the above śloka is: if the hole is narrowed, the sound becomes lower than its place, and if the hole is made bigger, the sound becomes higher than its place, that is its śruti. But this raising and lowering of the sound will be limited to four śrutis at most. Taking advantage of this procedure, we can also gain ease in the rakhāv (placement) of the fingers.
A hole that has slipped from its proper place is corrected by enlarging it; a hole that has risen from its proper place, by pariśodhana (correction) through making it smaller.
blocks.verse:
स्वस्थानाच्च्युतछिद्रस्य वृद्दधया शुद्धि र्विधीयते।
स्वस्थानोद्गत छिद्रस्य लाघवात् परिशोधनम्।।२७।।

blocks.text: That is, holes that have fallen from their proper place are corrected by making them bigger, and holes that have risen, by making them smaller. Here, the place of śuddha Dhaivata that has been fixed by calculation should in fact, by the test of the ear, be somewhat further down. But if that is done, it may be hard to place a finger on some large flute, and to find that proper place one would have to resort to laborious calculation. So to avoid these two difficulties we have raised Dhaivata a little and made it narrower, and lowered Ṣaḍja a little and made it wider, and accordingly put forward a simple form of the calculation. The further placing of the notes is as follows.
By the measure from Dhaivata to śuddha Niṣāda, Ṛṣabha is wanted above Ṣaḍja.
blocks.verse:
धैवतात्तु निषादस्य शुदस्य यावती मितिः।
तन्मानेन षड्जादूर्घ्वम् रिषभ इष्यते।।२८।।

blocks.text: That is, at whatever distance śuddha Niṣāda lies from śuddha Dhaivata, Ṛṣabha's place is at that same height above Sa.
By the measure from Ṣaḍja to Dhaivata, tīvra Madhyama [is placed] from Ṛṣabha; and between the two the wise should place śuddha Gāndhāra.
blocks.verse:
षड्जधैवतमानेन ऋषभात्तीव्र मध्यमः।
तयोर्मध्ये च गान्धारः शुद्धस्थाप्यो मनीषिभिः।।२९।।

blocks.text: Measure the distance from Sa down to Dhaivata, and place tīvra (sharp) Madhyama that same height above Ṛṣabha, and śuddha Gāndhāra in the middle between Sa and tīvra Ma′.
Between tīvra Madhyama and Gāndhāra is śuddha Madhyama; between Ṛṣabha and Ṣaḍja komal Ṛṣabha is held [to lie].
blocks.verse:
तीव्र मध्यम गान्धार मध्ये स्याच्छुद्ध मध्यमः।
ऋषभ षड्ज मध्ये तु कोमलो ऋषभोमतः।।३०।।

blocks.text: Between tīvra (sharp) Madhyama and Gāndhāra, śuddha Madhyama; and between Ṛṣabha and Ṣaḍja, komal Ṛṣabha: this is the proper placing.
Between Ṛṣabha and Gāndhāra komal Gāndhāra is held [to lie]. This is the order of the twelve notes here.
blocks.verse:
रिषभ गान्धारयोर्मध्ये गान्धारः कोमलो मतः।
क्रम एषः स्वराणाम् तु द्वादशानाम् भवेदिह।।३१।।

blocks.text: Between śuddha Ṛṣabha and Gāndhāra is the place of komal Ga. In this way the marks for the order of the 12 notes have been fixed here. Now the whole process of making is described once more in brief. First of all, measure the inner girth of the pipe or bamboo in the shape of a paper ring and open it out; the length of that bamboo should be from 9 to 10 times that. Then at one-ninth of it make the hole (surākh) of the mukharandhra (mouth-hole), its roundness one-third of the paridhimāna (measure of the circumference).

Then make a stopper of rubber, or of anything that can go inside, push it in, and bring it right up near the mouth-hole. Then blow into the mouth-hole and see whether, as the breath is increased, sounds of the kind Sa Ṡa Ṗa Ṡa come out in order. If it is right, then go on to place the notes in order by the method given above. Before placing them, take the sound that comes out by itself as mandra (lower) Pañcama; first draw a straight line, divide it into 10 parts up to the mouth-hole, and place madhya Pañcama at 4/10. Then place Sa between P̣a and Pa, Dha between Sa and P̣a, and komal Ni and Ni between Dha and Sa, and in the way described above make marks for all the notes.
For ease of the fingers a hole sometimes leaves its proper place; and for ease of the hand the holes are sometimes set out of line.
blocks.verse:
अंगुली लाघवार्थ हि क्वचित् स्वस्थान लंघनम्।
हस्त लाघवमादाय छिद्राणाम् वक्रता क्वचित्।।३२।।

blocks.text: Sometimes, when making a large flute, one also has to think whether, if the holes are made according to the marks fixed at their proper places, there will be special difficulty in placing the fingers. If there will be, some remedy is needed for that too. The above śloka gives the solution to this. First divide this difficulty into two parts: (1) the distance between the holes being greater than the spread of the fingers; (2) because the fingers are unequal, the short finger not reaching level with the long finger. Now for the first difficulty we can move the holes a little up or a little down from their fixed place; but when moving one down, do not forget to make it bigger as well, and when moving one up, to make the hole smaller than its fixed limit. In the same way, for the second difficulty we can move the holes to the right and left of the straight line. In this procedure the hole need not be made larger or smaller than its proper limit, because holes moved to the right or left of the line undergo no change in their sound. For this reason the hole of madhya Pañcama is made on the opposite side of the line, and it is closed with the thumb. Now the limits of the holes are considered: how much widening or narrowing of which hole can be justified.
By the measure of the inner circumference, the mouth-hole is one-third; the same measure is set for the holes that serve two notes.
blocks.verse:
अन्तः परिधिमानेन मुख रन्ध्ररूत्रयांशकः।
मानं तदेव छिद्राणाम् द्विस्वराणाम् प्रकल्पितम्।३३।

blocks.text: The opening of the mukharandhra (mouth-hole) will be at most a tṛtīyāṃśa (one-third) of the paridhimāna (measure of the circumference). And the sizes of the dvisvara chidras (holes serving two notes) will also be the same or a little less.
When the two Niṣādas are made [as separate holes], they will be one-fourth; when both Gāndhāras are made, they will be one-fifth.
blocks.verse:
निषादद्वय कल्पे तु चतूर्थाशौ भविष्यतः।
गान्धारोभय कल्पे तु पंचमांश भविष्यतः।३४।

blocks.text: If the Niṣādas are divided into two holes, both holes will be a quarter of the paridhimāna (measure of the circumference). If the Gāndhāras are divided into two holes, both holes will be a pañcamāṃśa (one-fifth) of the paridhimāna, 1/5.
The holes of Re, Dha and Ma are holes for two notes; the measure for Ṣaḍja and Pañcama is declared to be one-fourth.
blocks.verse:
रिध मानां च छिद्राणि द्विस्वराणि भवन्ति हि।
षड्ज पंचमयोर्मानाम् चतुर्यांश मुदाह्रतम्।३५।

blocks.text: That is, the holes made for Re, Dha and Ma should be made large, taking each as the place of two notes. Sa and Pa are acala (fixed notes), so small holes will suit them. Here by the hole of Pa is meant the last hole. Although the first hole too is the place of P̣a, this hole may also be natural. If an unnatural hole is to be made, it will have to be kept somewhat larger than the other holes.
If the bamboo is long, the hole there is held to be small; if the bamboo is short like a dwarf, the hole there is held to be large.
blocks.verse:
यदि प्रलम्बो बंशः स्याछिद्रं तत्र लघुस्मृतम्।
यदि वामनवद् बंशश्छिद्रं तत्र गुरुस्मृतम्।३६।

blocks.text: That is, if the bamboo is 10 times its paridhimāna (measure of the circumference), all the holes will be laghu (small). If it is seven times instead of ten, its holes will be large.

If this is not done, there is a chance of out-of-tuneness in Gāndhāra and Madhyama of the tāra saptaka (upper octave). In a flute where both forms of Niṣāda depend on a single hole, that hole will have to be kept somewhat larger than the Dhaivata hole. And in a flute where two holes are wanted for the two Niṣādas, both holes can be kept the same as Dhaivata's, or even a little smaller. So it is better to give all the holes a small form first, and afterwards make them bigger, matching them against a harmonium or some reliable instrument. For the solution to this fine point is audible, not visible.
The Kinds of Flute
Three kinds of flute are chiefly recognised: the Jihvāvatī and the Kṛṣṇā, and the third is the Prākṛtī.
blocks.verse:
त्रयो भेदास्तु वंशीनाम् मुख्यतः परिचीयते।
जिह्वाती च कृष्णा ष तृतीया प्राकृती भवेत्।३७।

blocks.text: That is, by [the kind of] mukharandhra (mouth-hole) the flute is of three main kinds. Their names in order are: (1) Jihvāvatī (fipple flute) (2) Kṛṣṇā (transverse flute) (3) Prākṛtī. Now the merits and faults of each of these, one by one, are considered.
Of these, the first, the Jihvāvatī, is easy to play even for children; [but] it is defiled by the mouth, it carries a smell, and its breath and sound are fixed.
blocks.verse:
आद्या जिह्वाती तत्र सुवाधा बालकैरपि।
उच्छिष्टा गंधयुक्ता ष स्वासनाद नियन्त्रिता।३८।

blocks.text: That is, the Jihvāvatī flute is very easy to play; for this quality alone even children like it. But its various [faults] are not seen by everyone. Faults: (1) It is always jūṭhā (defiled by the mouth). So to some extent it is a cause of infectious disease. (2) If it is not washed again and again, it also smells bad, so that one does not feel like playing it. (3) The breath and the nāda (sound) are also fixed. That is, if the flute-maker has made it alpāhārī (taking little breath), that flute can be played only with little breath; if for some reason the player is not in a position to give little breath, he cannot play it. Besides these faults there is a fourth fault as well: in winter, as one goes on playing, water collects in the flute, so that its mouth-hole fills up and its very sound begins to vanish. In this situation the player flicks it like a pen to get the water out of its jihvā (fipple); by this action the flute may break, and a social offence is also possible. In each of the flutes above the condition of the mouth-hole is different, so even though the process of playing is the same, there is a difference in the act of blowing. So now let us attend to the merits and faults of the Kṛṣṇā, that is the āḍī bansī (transverse flute).
The Kṛṣṇā was made by Kṛṣṇa, the author of the Gītā and the great yogī; at the start it is hard to master, but in the end it gives joy.
blocks.verse:
कृष्णा तु निर्माता कृष्णै र्गीताकारैः सुयोगिभिः।
प्रारम्भे कष्टसाध्या सा परिणामें तु सुखप्रदा।३९।

blocks.text: That is, the Kṛṣṇā flute was made by Lord Yogeśvara Śrī Kṛṣṇa. So it has only this much fault, that at the start one has to practise it with hardship, and so some people grow weary of this hardship and give it up. But having got past that hardship, those sādhakas (practitioners) become all the happier. Merits: (1) Children think it useless and leave it alone. (2) It is not jūṭhā (defiled by the mouth). (3) With the practice of breath and lips its tone grows ever sweeter. Merit (4): This flute can be made with one's own hands. Not many tools are needed to make it: bring a bamboo or a PVC pipe from the market, close one end with a cork or rubber, mark the places of the holes and make the holes, even with the point of a pair of scissors, and the flute will be ready. (5) Depending on one's blowing, this flute can be played from the softest to the loudest sound, which is called volume; this comes easily in it. (6) If needed for an ensemble, it can be raised or lowered by the blowing to match. (So the Kṛṣṇā flute, having these many merits, is the best of all. Now let us look at the merits and faults of the prākṛtika (natural) flute.)
The Prākṛtī flute, which is held to be the Tripurā, has a peculiar way of blowing; it is simple to make, but it causes faults of mudrā (posture).
blocks.verse:
विशिष्टि चित्रफूत्कारा निर्माणे सरला भवेत्।
मुद्रादोषकरा बंशी प्राकृती त्रिपुरा मता।४०।

blocks.text: That is, the Tripurā flute is extremely simple to make, but from the point of view of practising its phūṅk (blowing) it is difficult. If someone succeeds with the blowing of the Kṛṣṇā flute in two days, he may need 10 days for the blowing of the Tripurā flute. Besides this, the mudrā doṣa (fault of posture) is also unavoidable. The third fault is that the length and width of the Tripurā can be managed up to a limit, but beyond that it becomes hard to draw a sound from it by blowing. So, because of these many faults, it has not spread. It is in use only in the jungle regions of Assam.

The author first took up the Jihvāvatī at the age of 12, the Tripurā at the age of 20, and the āḍī bansī (transverse flute) at the age of 30, and succeeded. The author judged the transverse flute to be the best, and with his own hands he has made about 50 flutes and, by way of research, tried out each flute for several months; he has made and played flutes of many materials, some of iron, some of brass, some of aluminium and so on. These days, since 1978, he mostly makes and plays flutes of bamboo and sometimes of PVC pipe. He has various flutes, from the notes of the harmonium's kālī 1 (first black key) up to the very high (ati-tār) Ṣaḍja at its kālī 2. So, as samples, he is setting out the length, width and so on of some flutes, so that other sādhakas (practitioners) too, if they wish, can easily take it up, and by making flutes in all keys can win renown in various programmes.
Here the kinds of flute by fewer or more holes are written down: six-holed, seven-holed, and likewise eight- and nine-holed.
blocks.verse:
न्यूनाधिक्येन छिद्राणाम् वंशी भेदोऽत्र लिख्यते।
षट्छिद्रा सप्तछिद्रा च तथाष्ट नव छिद्रिका।४१।

blocks.text: Broadly, the flute is of three kinds. (1) The Jihvāvatī, in which a jibbhī (fipple) is fitted. (2) The Kṛṣṇā flute, in which a round mukharandhra (mouth-hole) is made. (3) The Tripurā, in which no separate hole is made for blowing and one has to blow through the natural opening itself; it is also called the prākṛta (natural) flute. But here, on the basis of fewer or more holes, four kinds each of all the flutes named above are being described.

# Ṣaṭchidrā (six-hole flute) - in which the work of 12 notes is done with only 6 holes. # Saptachidrā (seven-hole flute) - in which 12 notes are arranged in 7 holes. # Aṣṭachidrā (eight-hole flute) - in which 12 notes are arranged in 8 holes. # Navachidrā (nine-hole flute) - in which 12 notes are arranged in 9 holes.
In six-holed flutes the seven śuddha notes are set; in seven-holed flutes two Niṣādas are provided.
blocks.verse:
षट्छिद्रासु बंशीषु शुद्धाः सप्त्स्वरा मताः।
सप्त छिद्रासु बंशीषु निषादौ द्वौ प्रकल्पितौ।४२।

blocks.text: That is, in flutes that have 6 holes only the śuddha (natural) notes are placed. The remaining notes come out sādhanādhīna (by skill, by opening a hole halfway). But in the seven-hole flute separate holes are made for both forms of Niṣāda, komal and śuddha.
In eight-holed flutes the two Gāndhāras are provided; in nine-holed flutes Pa is held to stand in two places.
blocks.verse:
अष्ट छिद्रासु बंशीषु गान्धारद्वय कल्पना।
नव छिद्रासु बंशीषु पंचमौ द्विस्थितौ मतौ।४३।

blocks.text: That is, in the eight-hole bānsurī, along with Niṣāda, both Gāndhāras are also provided. And in the nine-hole flute there is provision for playing Pañcama from two places: one comes out with all the holes open, and the other with all the holes closed. This too is a marvel of this instrument which is not found in other instruments.

Of these two holes, from one only the Pa of the middle saptaka (octave) comes out, and from the other the Pa of all three octaves. The smallest āḍī bansī (transverse flute) I have is of aluminium pipe. If a small piece of that pipe were cut off, kept as a ring, and opened out flat, its length would be about one inch and one sūt (a small unit of length); this we can call the paridhimāna (measure of the inner circumference). The full length is seven inches and four sūt. Measured from the mukharandhra (mouth-hole) it is six inches four sūt. Its first hole is eight and a half sūt above the open (mukta) Pañcama at the bottom; this is taken as Dhaivata. The distance from Dhaivata to Niṣāda is 7 sūt. The distance from Niṣāda to Ṣaḍja, that is the third hole, is 4 sūt. The distance of Ṛṣabha, that is the fourth hole, from Ṣaḍja is six and a half sūt. Then Gāndhāra is five and a half from there, and the distance of tīvra Madhyama is 5 sūt. Thus the total distance from the open part at the bottom up to tīvra Madhyama at the top comes to thirty-six and a half sūt. In this flute, besides the six holes, there is a seventh hole too, for the Pañcama of the middle octave. Its distance from the tīvra Madhyama hole above is two and a half sūt, but this hole lies on the side opposite to the other holes, and it is easily closed with the thumb. Since this flute is not even seven times as long as its inner paridhimāna, the distances of its holes differ somewhat from the calculation given earlier. The hole distances given in the book are taken from the centre point. In this flute a separate hole for the komal notes would have been impractical, so players draw out 12 notes from only six [holes] by their skill. If the human finger were two sūt thinner, it could have had more holes. The Ṣaḍja that sounds in this flute when the top three holes are closed matches the upper (tār) octave of the harmonium's second black key. If the harmonium differs somewhat, the flute can be altered in the same proportion. Now the measurements of the larger flute, made for kālī 1 (the first black key), are written next.

The total length of this flute is 8 inches. Measured from the outside, the paridhi (circumference) is 15 sūt in all, that is one and a half inches. The inner circumference, that is the girth, is a little more than 11 sūt. The length from Pañcama to the mukharandhra (mouth-hole) is 6 inches 8 sūt. That is, from the mouth-hole down to the open (mukta) Pañcama this flute is six times its inner paridhimāna (measure of the inner circumference). It has 7 holes in all, of which one hole is at the back and six holes are on the front. The distance from the open Pañcama, that is the very end of the flute, to the first hole, that is Dhaivata, is nine sūt in all. The distance from the first hole to the second is less than seven sūt. The third hole is four sūt from there. The distance from the third to the fourth hole is six sūt. The distance from the fourth to the fifth hole is also six sūt. The distance from the fifth to the sixth hole is five and a half sūt. And the seventh, the hole made at the back, is at a distance of four sūt. Thus the total distance from mandra Pañcama to madhya Pañcama is about 9+6+6+5+4+4 sūt. From there the distance to the mouth-hole is 26 sūt.

If a flute is made on the basis of the measurements written above, eighty per cent of the flute will come out in tune. Yet it can be a hundred per cent right only when, matching those holes to the pitch of the harmonium, the golāī (roundness) of some holes is made smaller or larger by means of the pitch. A flute made on the basis of gaṇita (calculation) alone may also be incomplete, because working out the calculation for the roundness of a hole and making it on the basis of that calculation are both needlessly very difficult tasks. So, like salt in dāl, many tasks rest on estimate. So svara and Īśvara cannot be attained on the basis of calculation and logic. This is the meaning of the śloka written below.
Just as living beings do not reach God through the reasoning intellect, so the wise do not know the svaras through calculation alone.
blocks.verse:
तर्क बुध्या यथा जीवा नेश्वरम् प्रप्नुवन्ति हि।
तथा गणितमात्रेण बुधा जानन्ति न स्वरान।४४।

blocks.text: In the world svara and Īśvara are alike, pervading everywhere like the sky; tāla and kāla (time) are likewise, [passing] from the subtle into the gross, like fire.
blocks.verse:
स्वरेश्वरौ समौ लोके व्याप्तौ सर्वत्र व्योमवत्।
ताल कालौ तथैवास्तः सूक्ष्मात् स्थूलौ च वन्हिवत।४५।

blocks.text: This proves that what is bhāvagamya (known through feeling) is not buddhigamya (known through the intellect). From the earlier figure it is established that the lowest note of the flute, for which no hole other than the mukharandhra (mouth-hole) is needed, is the Pañcama of the mandra saptaka (lower octave), P̣a; and on this basis the holes of all the notes can be placed. In this, first, to find the middle Pañcama, we divide the length from the mouth-hole to the middle Pañcama in the ratio of 2-3, and fix the place of middle Pañcama at 2/5 from the mouth-hole. But if the pipe is only 6 times as long as its girth, or 5 and a half times as long, then in making its flute the place of Pañcama will need to be 3/8. Although between 2/5 and 3/8 there is so fine a difference that it can be evened out by enlarging or reducing the roundness of the hole, still this fineness is necessary for a special situation. The remaining notes will be placed in the way described earlier. If someone wants to place the 12 notes by dividing the length from P̣a to Pa into 12 equal parts, the flute will be out of tune. But if the pipe is tapered like a shehnai, the flute may come out right. This same point was written by the late Śrī Bhātkhaṇḍe ji: (uparyupari saṅkocastvākāśe bhavati dhruvam) [going higher and higher, a contraction surely occurs in the space]. Now, below, the length and width of the flutes from kālī 1 (first black key) to kālī 8 are written. Although harmoniums differ from one another by half a note or so, still some help can be had from this estimate. Here each length is 10 times its paridhimāna (measure of the inner circumference); but measured from the mouth-hole it will be 9 times. Just as the middle Pañcama, on the basis of mandra Pañcama and the mouth-hole, has been set not exactly midway between the two but between 2 and 3, in the same way it will be more suitable if the Ṣaḍja lying between the two Pañcamas is also not placed exactly in the middle but moved a little up towards Re; otherwise the mandra Pañcama will have to be made a baddha pañcama (bound Pa). If the last end of the pipe, which has been given the name mandra P̣a, is in its natural state, it is called mukta pañcama (open Pa). And if it is narrowed from inside with some ring, or more pipe is joined on beyond it and a large hole is made at the place of Pañcama, it is called baddha pañcama. Knowing of such a situation beforehand, skilled makers leave some part of the pipe or bamboo at the bottom and place mandra Pañcama [there]; if they do not do this, they divide the distance between P̣a and Pa into 13 equal parts and place Ṣaḍja between 6 and 7. The following śloka tells of these very two kinds of mandra Pañcama.
Kālī (black key) Length (inches) Width (sūt) 1 28 inches 28 sūt 2 26 26 sūt 3 21 1/2 21 sūt 4 19 19 sūt
Pa is said to be of two kinds, svayaṃbhūta (self-born) and kṛtrima (artificial); when the natural one cannot be managed, the artificial note is made.
blocks.verse:
पंचमस्तु द्विधा प्रोक्तः स्वयं भूतश्च कृत्रिमः।
स्वाभाविके त्वनिर्वाहे क्रियते कृत्रिमः स्वरः।४६।

blocks.text: This baddha pañcama (bound Pa) has other advantages too. For example, if after the flute is made any hole has to be made smaller or larger so that the notes pass the test of the ear, the baddha pañcama will remain under the maker's control. The second advantage is that if, while playing, the end of the flute touches some object or the seat by mistake, the Pañcama may be disturbed, but with the baddha pañcama this disturbance is impossible. The third advantage is that if the player, by his skill, wishes to use mandra Madhyama (Ṃa) in some rāga, [he can do so] by closing the baddha pañcama with the big toe. The length of the pipe or bamboo will be 10 times its paridhimāna (measure of the inner circumference); in it, placing the mouth-hole at the first part (1/10) from the top and mandra Pañcama at the first part (1/10) from the bottom, if the other notes are placed in the remaining eight parts, it will be excellent.
The Second Method of Making
One more method of making the flute, simpler than the one above, is given here. I myself make [flutes] by it. Its rules are set out in the following 7 ślokas
There is a second method too in the work of making the flute, by which those who seek tunefulness may find every convenience in the making.
blocks.verse:
द्वितीयोऽपि प्रकारः स्याद् बंशी निंर्माण कर्मणि।
निर्माणे येन सौविध्यं सर्वथा स्यात्सुरैषिणाम्।47।

blocks.text: At the start of the bamboo the mouth-hole is set, at the end of the bamboo stands Pa; and from the middle to the end all the notes are here fixed in order.
blocks.verse:
बंशादौ मुखरः प्रोक्तः बंशान्ते पंचमः स्थितः।
मध्यान्ते तु विनिर्णीताः क्रमात् सर्वे स्वरा इह।48।

blocks.text: That is, for the convenience of makers a second method is also being given. Here the mukharandhra (mouth-hole) is at the start of the bamboo, Pañcama (P̣a) at the end, and all the remaining notes are placed from the middle to the end. See Figure No. 16.
Divide the bamboo, measured up to the mouth-hole, into six parts; the first part from below is held to have two parts.
blocks.verse:
मुखरन्ध्रमितं वशम् षड्भागे परिकल्पयेत्।
अधस्तात् प्रथमों भागस्तस्मिन् भागद्वयं मतम्।49।

blocks.text: Divide the length from P̣a to the mukharandhra (mouth-hole) into six equal parts, and divide the first part from the bottom into two parts.
From the mandra Pa, at the end of the first [half] let ṛju (komal) Dhaivata be placed; above that, at the end of the second, śuddha Dhaivata is wanted.
blocks.verse:
मन्द्रपात् प्रथमस्यान्ते स्थाप्यताम् ऋजु धैवतः।
तत ऊर्ध्व द्वितीयान्ते शुद्ध धैवत इष्यते।50।

blocks.text: At the end of the first part from the bottom place komal Dhaivata, and at the end of the second, śuddha Dhaivata.
Dhaivata [is placed] after taking a sixth part away from the ṣaṣṭhāṃśa (one-sixth); but when the sixth is left undivided, Dhaivata is held to be at the [full] sixth.
blocks.verse:
षष्ठांशात् षष्ठमम् भागम् न्यूनंकृत्वा तु धैवतः।
अखण्डिते तु षष्ठांशे धैवतः षष्ठमे मतः।51।

blocks.text: If mandra Pañcama is open in the flute, then for the distance of Dhaivata, that is the first hole, above it: divide the ṣaṣṭhāṃśa (one-sixth) again into six parts, take one part away from it, and mark Dhaivata at whatever distance remains. Then, when making the hole, make it a small hole and enlarge it while testing the note. If Pañcama is not open but is made by a hole, the ṣaṣṭhāṃśa will remain whole.

But if the distance of the open Pañcama from the mouth-hole is nine 'miti', Dhaivata will be at the distance of the full ṣaṣṭhāṃśa (one-sixth). Take miti to mean paridhimāna (measure of the inner circumference).
The second sixth is held to have three parts; there let the two Niṣādas and Ṣaḍja be placed in order.
blocks.verse:
षष्ठांशे द्वितीये तु भागें भागत्रयम् मतम्।।
निषादौ द्वौ तथा षड्जः स्थाप्यन्ताम् क्रम पूर्वकम्।52।

blocks.text: Divide the second ṣaṣṭhāṃśa (one-sixth) into three parts and place, in order, the 3 notes komal Ni, Ni, Sa at equal distances.
The third sixth [has] four parts; there the two Ṛṣabhas and the two Gāndhāras are to be placed in order.
blocks.verse:
षष्ठांशे तृतीये तु भागें भाग चतुष्पृयम्।
रिषभौ द्वौ च गान्धारौ तत्र स्थाप्याः क्रमेण वै।53।

blocks.text: In the same way, divide the third ṣaṣṭhāṃśa (one-sixth) into four parts and place komal Re, Re, komal Ga, Ga.
The fourth sixth is divided into five parts; in the first three of these parts are the two Madhyamas and Pa.
blocks.verse:
षष्ठांशे चतुर्थेतु भागाः पंच प्रकल्पिताः।
तत्रादौ त्रिसु भागेषु मध्यमौ पंचमः स्मृताः।54।

blocks.text: And divide the fourth ṣaṣṭhāṃśa (one-sixth) into five parts and place Ma, Ma′ and Pa in the first, second and third parts, in order. Beyond this, by leaving out the [remaining] part, the place of Pa falls of itself at 2/5, as before. For these divisions you can take the help of paper; folding it will make the dividing easy. This method will suit only a length of nine times. If the length is near eight or seven times, then instead of the ṣaṣṭhāṃśa take the saptāṃśa (one-seventh): mark off four saptāṃśas from the bottom, and in those same four saptāṃśas make two, three, four and five divisions in order, and place the 12 notes.
Artificial Komal Notes
For the convenience of those who seek tunefulness, in rāgas with komal Re and Dha, an artificial komal Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata should be made on the instrument.
blocks.verse:
रिध कोमल रागेषु सौविध्याय सुरैषिणाम्।
कृत्रिमौ कोमलौ कार्यौ वाद्ये रिषभधैवतौ।55।

blocks.text: After the 12 notes in all have been placed in the flute by the rules above, a flute can be made and played, on the basis of those svarasthāna (note positions), with at least six and at most 10 holes. Even so, the problem of lifting half a finger for komal Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata could not be solved. So by a scientific method I made komal Re and Dha, and they also worked in playing. For this the holes of Re and Dha must be made smaller in some way. That device can be of any material: rubber, wood and so on.
Re and Dha should there be filled with a piece of a bead-string, or with some other wooden device, so that a small hole results.
blocks.verse:
माला खण्डेन वाऽन्र्येन काष्ठोपकरणेन च।
पूरणीयौ ऋधौ तत्र लघु छिद्रं यथा भवेत्।56।

blocks.text: This solution is possible in 3 ways. 1 Take one bead out of some mālā (string of beads) and seat it on the hole like a guṭakā (plug), so that the hole is closed like a phial [with its stopper]. Then the small hole of that plug should be enlarged only so far that the komal note is heard exactly right. But this procedure will not succeed in a six-hole bānsurī, because in it Re, on becoming komal, will spoil the Gāndhāra lying next to it. Although this difficulty occurs in the nine-hole flute too, in it a light chhallā (ring) is put into the separately made holes of komal Ga and Ni, and when Re and Dha are made komal those rings are removed. Or else bend a brass strip and put it inside the pipe, so that inside it fits to the very shape of the pipe, and by sliding it komal Gāndhāra can be brought back to how it was.
Their size should be from half to a third of the [original] measure, watching the thickness of the plug and watching the rāga again and again.
blocks.verse:
अर्धमानात् तृतीयांशः परिमाण स्तयोर्भवेत्।
पूरकस्थूलता म्पश्यन् रागं पश्यन् मुहुर्मुहुः।57।

blocks.text: That is, in the pūraka (plug, guṭakā) by which a hole is closed, a hole smaller than that hole, from half down to a quarter of it, should be made in that plug, and the hole should be enlarged according to the thickness of that plug. And while enlarging, enlarge it little by little, and keep testing its komal quality by playing rāga Bhairav or Toḍī again and again.

The second method of making this artificial Ṛṣabha is as follows. Shave that much of the pipe with something and make it smooth. Close the place, the part in which the Re and Ga holes lie, with a piece of some other pipe. Then, according to rāga Toḍī, make a small hole for Re and a large hole for komal Ga [in it]. Now, when that piece is turned, the holes beneath will be closed; then, in it, facing the holes of the original pipe beneath, let two holes be made according to śuddha Re and Ga. The four holes of that upper pipe, skilfully made, will turn by turns over the two holes beneath, and komal or śuddha notes will be formed as you wish. But some rāgas with both Ṛṣabhas will get no benefit from this artificial note. So for those rāgas one will have to adopt the mūrchanā paddhati (method of shifting Sa), changing Sa. For this artificial Re–

The third method is this: instead of putting a pipe over the pipe, if some thin piece of the same size is fitted inside the pipe, then by sliding the inner pipe one way the Re hole will become small and the Ga hole large, and by sliding it upward the Ga hole will become small and the Re hole large. But in this procedure air passes through because of the looseness, so the procedure does not succeed as well. Like Re and Dha, Ga and Ni too can be made artificial.

blocks.subsection_title: The Sound of the Bīn from the Flute
blocks.text: The Sound of the Bīn in the Flute

blocks.subsection_title: The Sound of the Bīn from the Flute
blocks.text: Near the mouth-hole let another hole be made; cover it with a membrane born of the bamboo itself, and play.
blocks.verse:
मुखरन्ध्र समीपे तु छिद्राऽन्यः परिकल्प्यताम्।
बंशजेनैव पत्रेण तमाच्छाद्य निनादयेत्।58।

blocks.subsection_title: The Sound of the Bīn from the Flute
blocks.text: The sound rising from the mouth-hole sets the bhojpatra vibrating; this gives the instrument a novel quality, and its tone becomes like Tumburu's.
blocks.verse:
मुखरन्ध्रोत्थितो नादो भोजपत्रं प्रकम्पयेत्।
वैचित्र्यं तेन वाद्यस्य ध्वनिः तुम्बुरुवद् भवेत्।59।

blocks.subsection_title: The Sound of the Bīn from the Flute
blocks.text: To change the sound of the flute into a sound like that of the bīn (reed pipe), that is the mahuar, another hole is made near the mukharandhra (mouth-hole), and it is closed by sticking bhojpatra (the thin inner membrane of bamboo) over it with gum. When that membrane vibrates with the sound of the flute, the flute's sound becomes like the bīn. But in this procedure special care must be taken of the weather, because under the effect of heat and cold the kampana (vibration) of the bhojpatra will sometimes be right in the tār saptaka (upper octave) and sometimes right in the mandra saptaka (lower octave). Meeting very dry air, the bhojpatra may also dry out and split. So, according to place and time, wise people can test it and benefit from it. In the āḍī bansī (transverse flute) it can be made, without a separate hole, by making the hole in its kārk (cork) itself, and by closing that with a second cork it can also be opened whenever one wishes; in this way that second cork does the work of a sañcālikā (switch). Just as the jawārī of the bridge works in the sitar, so is the importance of bhojpatra in the flute. So nature has produced bhojpatra inside the bamboo itself. If you split some bamboo while it is still fresh and look, the white membrane stuck to the bamboo inside it, which is especially thin and soft, is what is called bhojpatra. In the transverse flute, a little away from the mouth-hole, [the tube] is closed by fitting a stopper; that is what is called the cork. Some people keep the bamboo's node itself and use it as the stopper, but this does not work very well, so the use of a separate soft material such as rubber, sponge or a bottle cork is what everyone accepts. When putting it in, the bamboo is tied with thick thread; otherwise the bamboo may split.

blocks.subsection_title: Here Begins the Section on Practice
blocks.text: Sādhanā Khaṇḍa (Part on Practice)

blocks.subsection_title: Here Begins the Section on Practice
blocks.text: Now the chapter on sādhanā (practice)

blocks.subsection_title: Here Begins the Section on Practice
blocks.text: By the syllable sa the body is meant; dha [stands for concentration]; by na the life-breath is understood: [so] sādhanā has the nature of the three guṇas.
blocks.verse:
सकारेण शरीरः स्याद् धकारो भवेत्।
नकारेण स्मृतः प्राणः साधना त्रिगुणात्मिका।६०।

blocks.subsection_title: Here Begins the Section on Practice
blocks.text: Broadly, the meaning of sādhanā is the activity that leads from ignorance towards knowledge. Even so, here the author's own intent is given, which is set out in this śloka on the basis of scientific truth. Until body, mind and prāṇa (life-breath) are brought in one direction and one sets out from comfort towards discomfort, there can be no sādhanā of any subject. So, (sa) for śarīra (body), dha for dhāraṇā (concentration) and na for prāṇa: thus, by including body, mind and prāṇa in sādhanā, sādhanā has been described as having the three guṇas, sattva, rajas and tamas.

blocks.subsection_title: Here Begins the Section on Practice
blocks.text: Through balanced āhāra and vihāra, and keeping to the vow of brahmacarya, one should patiently train the breath, the tongue and the fingers.
blocks.verse:
युक्ताहार विहाराभ्याम ब्रम्हचारि व्रते स्थितः।
प्राण जिह्वांगुलीयांञ्च साधयेद् धैर्य पूर्वकम।६१।

blocks.subsection_title: Here Begins the Section on Practice
blocks.text: That is, delighting in the five objects taken in through the body's five organs of knowledge is called āhāra (intake), and the activities done through the five organs of action are called vihāra (conduct). To sift these two through far-sightedness and fine discernment and to keep the mind in control over them is itself a yoga. Practice of the flute too is not possible without yoga.

blocks.subsection_title: Here Begins the Section on Practice
blocks.text: Along with this, to remove the natural restlessness of the mind, it will be necessary to look upon the various feelings towards many many-coloured things and persons, in the light of knowledge, with a sense of oneness. The essence of all things and persons seen in this way is called Brahman. One who moves the mind in That is called a brahmacārī. To take care of the body's subtle but precious element, that is to protect the vīrya (semen), is also a principal part of brahmacarya (continence, discipline). In common usage a one-sided form of brahmacarya is current; in the sādhanā (practice) of the flute this is necessary.

blocks.subsection_title: Here Begins the Section on Practice
blocks.text: So, by reforming āhāra and vihāra in this way, try to bring simplicity into life. Then, while keeping brahmacarya, one should practise the prāṇa (breath), jihvā (tongue) and fingers by the methods below. Bear in mind that with a feeling of śraddhā (reverence) sādhanā becomes easy, whereas with a feeling of envy sādhanā becomes harsh. A feeling of hatred or envy towards any person, or of greed for any thing or position, arises of itself. To regard these as destroyers of the yajña (sacrifice) of sādhanā and to disregard them, and to keep setting up again and again in the mind the feeling of reverence towards knowledge, is the sādhaka's mental yajña.

blocks.subsection_title: Here Begins the Section on Practice
blocks.text: One should purify the path of the breath by pūraka, kumbhaka and recaka (inhalation, retention and exhalation); the tongue by pronouncing ṭa and ka; and the fingers by exercise.
blocks.verse:
प्राणस्य सोधयेन्मांर्गम् पूरक कुम्भक रेचकैः।
टकावुच्यार्य जिह्वांश्च व्यायामेनांगुलीयकान्।६२।

blocks.subsection_title: Here Begins the Section on Practice
blocks.text: That is, one should perfect the prāṇa (breath) by prāṇāyāma (breath control), the tongue by ṭa and ka, and the fingers by vyāyāma (exercise).
Sādhanā of the Prāṇa (Practice of the Breath)

Broadly, for the sādhanā (practice) of the breath other ācāryas have taught this procedure: pūraka (drawing [the breath] up), kumbhaka (holding the breath) and recaka (letting the breath out slowly). But for flute players this procedure is mastered effortlessly anyway. So one should especially practise bhastrikā prāṇāyāma, that is (moving the breath up and down at a fast pace for 2 minutes), so that a sweet kampana (vibration) arises in the nāda (sound). As when, after a gong is struck, a beautiful wave-like vibrating sound is heard for a while, that is called uttama (excellent) vibration. As a lamp's flame wavers in a light breeze, so an adhama (poor) vibration lives naturally, as a fault, in the notes of all sādhakas (practitioners); this vibration is wholly to be given up. And regular vibration is wholly to be taken up. This procedure is like levelling the natural unevenness of barren land and making a regular rise and fall in the form of beautiful garden beds. Only then will the plants of the notes look beautiful in that bed. Do this procedure daily in the early morning in the winter days, increasing it from 2 minutes to 5 minutes. Then if you make the sound vibrate regularly on any one note of the flute, a single note will keep the mind immersed in bliss.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Practice of the tongue

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: It is proven by experience that touching the jihvā (tongue) in turn to the throat, the palate, the roof of the mouth and the teeth produces the sounds (ka), (ca), (ṭa) and (ta). In the same way, keep blowing into the flute while saying ṭa and ka quickly and without a break, many times over. Just as the dir dir of the sitar turns one note into equal pieces, so [this] will make the sound coming out of the flute beautiful with equal strokes. If at first some fault is heard in the breath because of this action, do not be put off by it; keep practising for a long time, with confidence, like this: (ṭa ka ṭa ka ṭa ka). Once it is mastered, it will become beautiful. These same two syllables will turn Sa into Sa Sa Sa Sa and Re into Re Re Re Re.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: If, instead of ṭa-ka, one relies on some other syllable such as ca or ta, the practitioner will regret it later, because along with the breath the saliva must also be kept in check.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Practice of the fingers

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: It is true that the fingers gain strength from repeatedly and quickly gripping something and letting it go; this natural exercise goes on anyway in various tasks such as washing clothes. But because in these tasks there is no devotion to the exercise, or absorption in it, we do not give it the place of sādhanā (practice). So, with the fingers held straight on a table and without moving the hand, keep striking with just one finger, with full strength, a hundred times in a row, counting; then strike with the second, third and fourth finger in the same way. Then close the holes on the flute and, in the same way, keep striking each finger quickly on the hole of the flute until pain arises at the root of the finger. Then strike two fingers together, and then three fingers together. By doing this every day without a break, the speed of the fingers will keep increasing month by month, and this will give you good help in the svara practice that comes later. Then, if you also want to learn another instrument, such as the tabla, you will progress quickly in that too. The following śloka points to these very things.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: In a tantu vādya (stringed instrument) there is kampa (vibration), and it is seen with the eyes; but the vibration in a vāyu vādya (wind instrument) is understood by inference.
blocks.verse:
तन्तु वाद्ये भवेत्कम्पः नेत्राभ्याम् स विलोक्यते।
वायु वाद्ये तु यः कम्पः सोऽनुमानेन बुध्यते।६३।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That is, in instruments such as the vīṇā and the sitar the string is made to vibrate by the hand, so we can see that kampana (vibration) with our eyes. But the flute is a vāyu vādya (wind instrument): the air from the mouth sets up vibration in the air inside the flute, so we can establish that vibration only by reasoning (anumāna, inference). For it is a scientific truth that nāda (musical sound) cannot arise without vibration. Only a thing that has lacāva (elasticity) can vibrate. A string has elasticity, so it vibrates. Air too has elasticity, so it vibrates. But the vibration of a string differs from the vibration of air in direction. If the string's vibration is across its width, the air's vibration is along its length. The string's length is tied to the pegs and is tightened, but the air's width is bound and held tight by the bamboo. So if the bamboo cracks for some reason, the air is no longer held tight and no sound is produced. Like air, water too is elastic, so the jal taraṅg is a successful instrument. But water cannot vibrate without the support of air, and in the same way a string does not vibrate without the support of air. So for vibration the support of air has to be taken. In the flute, air is made to vibrate by air, in air. In stringed instruments, material is made to vibrate by material, in air. In instruments such as the shehnai, material is made to vibrate by air, in air. In covered instruments (such as the mṛdaṅga), skin is made to vibrate by the hands, in air. The saying (jātaḥ prāṇāgni saṃyogāt) [it is born from the union of breath and fire] is a scientific truth.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Pravāhita (flowing), alpabaddha (slightly confined) and mukta (free): air is of these three kinds, and these are the causes of the production of sound in an instrument made of bamboo and the like.
blocks.verse:
प्रवाहितोऽल्प बद्धश्च मुक्तश्चेति त्रिधानिलाः।
बंशादि निर्मिते वाद्ये नादस्योत्पत्तिहेतवः।६४।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Whatever metal the flute may be made of, the nāda (musical sound) in it arises only from air. Here air is of three kinds. The first is pravāhita (flowing): the air that flows from the player's mouth as breath through a very narrow passage and is confined on all sides. The second is (alpabaddha, slightly confined): the air that fills the inside of the flute. And the third is (mukta, free): the air through which the sound is able to reach the listeners' ears. Seen this way, living beings too fall into these same three classes: 1 animals, 2 humans, 3 gods. But to see the whole world as a flute, I would have to reach the level of a flute player. Now we write the features and kinds of the most confined air.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: The issuing of air from the mouth is called phūtkāra (blowing). It is prākṛta (natural) and vaikṛta (cultivated), and the third is kṛtrima (artificial).
blocks.verse:
मुखतो वायु निर्धातः फूत्कार इति कथ्यते।
प्राकृतो वैकृतश्चैव कृत्रिमस्तु तृतीयकः।६५।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That is, the directed issue, that is, the flow, of air from the mouth is called phūtkāra, that is, phūṅk (blowing). It has three kinds: prākṛta (natural), vaikṛta (cultivated) and kṛtrima (artificial). The Tripurā flute is played with natural blowing, the āḍī (transverse) flute with cultivated blowing, and the flute with a jibbhī (fipple) with artificial blowing. For natural blowing no mukharandhra (mouth-hole) of any kind has to be made in the flute; the sound is made by the player's skill alone. For cultivated blowing a mouth-hole and a cork have to be provided, and the player makes [the breath] fit for sound with some effort. For artificial blowing the flute maker has to make all the effort, and the player gets the sound out easily. Man follows the middle path, so for him cultivated blowing is the best.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Cultivated blowing is the best; natural blowing is held to be middling; blowing that relies on an inert device is faulty and is the lowest.
blocks.verse:
फूत्कारों वैकृतः श्रेष्ठः प्राकृतो मध्यम स्मृतः।
जड़ाश्रितस्तु फूत्कारो दोष यक्तोऽधमो भवेत्।६६।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Whatever the kind of blowing, the cause of nādotpatti (the production of sound) in the flute is only the friction of air. When moving air strikes, many kinds of vibration begin in the still air. Differences in the fixed width and length of the air bring rise and fall in the sound. This very rise and fall is given the name sargam (the scale of notes). The following śloka says just this.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Sent into the mukharandhra (mouth-hole), the phūtkāra (breath) becomes the rubbing [agent]; the still air, rubbed by it, gives rise to nāda (musical sound).
blocks.verse:
मुखरन्ध्रे विनिक्षिप्तः फूत्कारो घर्षको भवेत्।
तेन घृष्टोऽचलो वायुस्तेन नादः प्रजायते।६७।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: So, for sound to arise in any flute, the rubbing air, that is, the phūṅk (breath), must be slanting. If the flow of the rubbing [air] becomes strong, the vibration of the air begins to increase in the order of twofold, threefold and fourfold. This action cannot be seen with the eyes, but as a result of these actions the ears hear in the sounds the difference Sa Ṡa Ṗa Ṡa. So we infer that in the enclosed air inside the flute the capacity to vibrate takes many forms, depending on the length of the flute. So with slackness or strength in the flow of the breath, the capacity changes at once. Now, leaving this subtlety to the scientists, I must move on to the elements that concern the practice of music. So, about the qualities of the breath in the flute —

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Calm in appearance, long-breathed, with a steady gaze, making a good sound; with head and body not too bent; controlled in the low and high registers;
blocks.verse:
सौम्याकृतिः, प्रलम्बासुः समदृष्टिः, सुनादकृत्।
नातिवक्र, शिरः कायो, मन्द्रतार नियन्त्रितः।६८।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: free of hissing, fine, held under control at the mukharandhra (mouth-hole), and well vibrated: blowing should be known to have these ten qualities.
blocks.verse:
सीतकार रहितः, सूक्ष्मों, मुखरन्ध्र वशीकृतः।
सुकम्पितश्च फूप्कारो ज्ञेयो दशगुणान्वितः।६९।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: The breath for the flute has the ten qualities above, and opposite to them there can be as many faults. The practitioner has to avoid the faults and move towards the qualities; those qualities are explained here. — (1) While blowing, the face should be pleasant and calm. (2) The breath should come out for a long time. (3) The gaze should be steady and the eyes open naturally. (4) There should be sweetness in the breath. (5) The body should not be too bent. (6) The breath should be so controlled that the notes of the mandra (low), madhya (middle) and tāra (high) saptaka (octave) can be produced at will. (7) The face should not be distorted while blowing. (8) No kind of hissing should be heard with the breath, or before or after it. (9) The stream of the breath should be so thin that it can produce sound even in small holes. (10) There should be a regular vibration in the breath that is heard like a wave. — All these qualities are for the āḍī (transverse) and the Tripurā flute.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: For the flute with a jībh (fipple) the following points should be kept in mind. (1) Do not take the flute far into the mouth; as far as possible, keep it at the front edge of the lips. (2) Tighten the breath in proportion to the room there is in the jibbhī (fipple) built inside the flute, so that there is control over the sounds of two octaves. (3) Saliva should not come along with the breath. — The above qualities and faults should be watched closely in the early period. Some people even make use of a mirror.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: If one listens carefully to the sound of one's own breath, an irregular vibration will be seen in the sound, like the flickering flame of a lamp. Taking that as a fault, several actions for regular vibration are described in the following śloka.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Vibration of the heart, vibration of the throat, vibration of the root of the tongue, and likewise vibration of the adhara (lips); and sometimes the fingertips are made to vibrate.
blocks.verse:
हृत्कम्पःकण्ठः कम्पश्च जिह्वा मूलस्य कम्पनम्।
तथैवाधर कम्पश्च कराग्रौ कम्पितौ क्वचित्।७०।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That is, the vibration that comes from an exercise like the way a dog keeps panting in the hot season is called hṛtkampa, that is, heart vibration. For the flute this is the best vibration. Some people make the vibration with the throat — that is middling. And some people make the lips or the hands vibrate — this is the lowest. The practitioner should practise the best kind of breath close to a guru (teacher), for otherwise one does not see one's own faults. To blow into the Tripurā flute, one should close the open end of the bamboo from three sides and blow slantwise from one side; it is mainly because the breath is connected with three sides that it is named Tripurā. This is what the following śloka says.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Where the blowing is accomplished by covering three parts [of the opening], the wise therefore call that flute the Tripurā.
blocks.verse:
भागत्रयम् प्रपूयैंर्व फूतकारो यत्र साध्यते।
अतस्ताम् त्रिपुराम् बंशीम् कथयन्ति मनीषिणः।७१।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Some practitioners blow the flute two or four times, fail, and lose heart; so an effort is being made to awaken their enthusiasm again.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Leaving the instrument aside, one should first direct the breath at fire and the like; then the breath perfected there should be properly applied to the instrument.
blocks.verse:
वाद्यम् विहाय फूत्कारम् पावकादौ न्यसेत्पुरा।
तत्र सिध्दम् हि फूत्कारम् वाद्ये सभ्यक् प्रसाधयेत्।७२।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That is, a new practitioner should first practise blowing at a fire; when the practice of blowing at a fire has been mastered over a week, then one should try for sound in the flute with that breath. For when the lips are not balanced, the flow of the breath becomes crooked, and when too much air comes out in the breath, the breath does not last.
