So, to make the stream of the breath long, thin and straight, it will be right, on spiritual, scientific and Vedic evidence, to regard Agni deva (the god of fire) himself as the very first guru (teacher). Śrī Manu, the author of the dharmaśāstra, has also given fire the place of guru: (gururagnirdvijātīnām) [fire is the guru of the twice-born]; (tamaso mā jyotirgamaya) [lead me from darkness to light]. All these sayings create faith in fire in us, and through faith both skill and knowledge become easy to gain. In this way, by trying many times, the breath is mastered and begins to produce a beautiful sound in the flute in a balanced way. If the flow of the breath is joined to the mukharandhra (mouth-hole) on the flute, there can be three kinds of it, of which only the third kind is correct; the other two kinds are incorrect. Look at the figure below and try.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: The flow of the breath keeps spreading out like light —

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: I hope these figures will be of proper benefit to practitioners.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: The Jihvāvatī (duct flute) with a good jihvā (fipple) should be sounded with the front of the mouth; [it should be one] that has passed the test of the middle and high [registers] and has sweet notes.
blocks.verse:
जिह्वावतींम् सुजिह्वां तु मुखाग्रेण निनादयेत्।
मध्यतार परीक्षाया मुत्तीर्णाम् सरस, स्वराम्।७३।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: In the āḍī (transverse) flute or the Tripurā flute the sweetness of the breath depends on the practitioner, but in the Jihvāvatī (duct flute) the sweetness of the breath depends mostly on the maker, and making it is somewhat difficult. So it will be best, for the most part, to buy a flute with a jībh (fipple) from the market, because that maker's hand is practised in making it. Even so, the faults that are possible should be tested for at the time of buying. If there is no hissing in the breath and all seven notes come out properly in both octaves, it will be right to buy such a flute from the market and play it. While playing, only the front part of the mouth should touch it; and, avoiding again and again faults of posture such as puffing the cheeks and shutting the eyes, one should practise on the notes of both octaves with the help of 'ṭa' or 'ka' on the tongue. Now some light is thrown on the rakhāva (placement) of the fingers.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Three [holes] with the fingers of the right [hand], three with the fingers of the left: this is the covering of the holes laid down for the ṣaṭsvarā (six-note flute).
blocks.verse:
दक्षिणांगुलिभि स्तृाणि तृीणि बामांगुलीयकैः।
प्राच्छादनं तु छिद्राणाम् षट् स्वरायाम् प्रकल्पितम्।७४।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That is, if the flute has six holes, the three upper holes should be closed with three fingers of the right hand, and the three lower holes with three fingers of the left hand. Keep in mind that the fingers should be as straight as possible, because if they are bent, success in practising the komal notes will later be hard to achieve. If the middle part of the middle finger is on the hole, the other two fingers will straighten by themselves. But if the flute is large, the fingers have to be slanted somewhat because of the distance between the holes. Even then, no finger should be raised in the middle and bent at the tip. It will be better if this too is done under a guru's guidance. Otherwise many kinds of faults and doubts will unsettle the practitioner. Now the placement of the fingers on nine holes is described.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Then players cover the fourth and the eighth [holes] with the little fingers; and practitioners keep the thumb on the hole placed on the opposite side.
blocks.verse:
तूर्याष्टमौ कनिष्ठाभ्याम् वादकाश्छादयन्त्यथ।
विपरीतस्थितेडङ्गुष्ठां छिद्रे रक्षन्ति साधकाः।७५।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: The holes should be covered in the earlier order with the fingers beginning with the index finger, keeping them straight, or sometimes slightly bent.
blocks.verse:
पूर्वक्रमेण छिद्राणि तर्जन्याद्यंगुलीयकैंः।
प्राच्छादयेदवक्रेण स्वल्प वक्रेण वा क्वचित्।७६।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That is, closing the holes in order from the top with the index and the other fingers according to the earlier rule, in a flute with eight holes close the fourth and the eighth holes with the kaniṣṭhā, that is, the smallest fingers. If, besides the eight, there is a ninth hole from the bottom on the opposite side, close it with the thumb. If, when making the flute, the holes are made with the placement of the fingers in mind, the holes will not all lie in a straight line but will certainly look somewhat crooked; but this brings quick success in practice and does no harm. If, tempted by good looks, the holes are set in a straight line, crookedness will come into the placement of the fingers, and that could stand in the way of success. That is why practitioners today feel hardship on large flutes. It was largely to solve these very difficulties that the late Śrī Pannalal Ghosh ji had his fingers lengthened by surgery. This was certainly a sign of his boundless devotion, but for his followers it became a hard nut to crack.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: The solution I have found for this will be scientifically acceptable to all. If a separate hole is made between Dha and Ni for komal Ni, and between Re and Ga for komal Ga, there are three benefits: (1) the distance between the holes becomes smaller; (2) clarity comes easily in rāgas with komal notes; (3) greater success is gained in the action of mīṇḍ (glide). So practitioners are requested to make and practise on a nine-hole flute from the very beginning. This is made clear in the figure ahead. Here figure (7) is for those who like to keep the left hand below. Figure (8) is for those with the opposite preference. We have made this design after checking carefully that it poses no difficulty for the placement of human fingers. Here the hole at the very top is for placing the thumb, so by giving it a place on the edge of the flute it is shown that the thumb too is placed not fully at the back but pressed to the right or the left. If you feel some discomfort, you can make the rows of holes more crooked or straighter, depending on the thickness of the flute. This will make no difference to the notes, because the difference between the notes depends on the distance between the holes and on the size of the holes.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: At the start, practitioners should practise on a flute one hasta (cubit) long, measured by their own arm. Then after one year it will be right to practise on one of one and a half hastas, and after two years on a flute of about two hastas. This process will lead the placement of the fingers naturally towards progress. See the length of the flute, according to the tastes of the three stages of life — childhood, youth and maturity — in the ślokas written below.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Children take delight in the high register, the young in the middle octave; and in mature players the delight arises in the low [register].
blocks.verse:
बालानाम् तु रुचि स्तारे युवानाम् मध्य सप्तके।
प्रौणानाम् वादकानाम् तु रुचिर्मन्द्रे प्रजायते।७७।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That is, children like a flute of the tāra (high) octave, young people one of the madhya (middle) octave, and mature people one of the mandra (low) octave.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: The Tārī (small, high-pitched flute) measures half a hasta (cubit), the Madhyā (medium flute) one hasta; the Mandrā (large, low-pitched flute) should be one and a half hastas, and sometimes even two hastas.
blocks.verse:
हस्तार्ध परिमिता तारी मध्या हस्तैक मानका।
सार्धहस्ता भवेन्मन्द्रा द्विहस्ताऽपि क्वचित।७८।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: It is a proof of the Supreme Lord's wondrous glory that whatever is good for a creature is also what it likes. So animals and birds give up food when they are sick. So in childhood there is a natural liking for the Tārī flute (of the high octave), and in youth for the Madhyā flute (of the middle octave). This too is a special feature of the flute. If the placement of the fingers is to be kept up, it will be best to practise on a small flute from childhood. In the above śloka the dimensions of all three flutes are given. The Tārī flute is half a hasta (cubit) long, the Madhyā one hasta long and the Mandra one and a half hastas long. Here and there, practitioners with long fingers even play a flute two hastas long.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Covering the holes with the part of the finger just short of its end is praised; one should not press on the flute's holes with the very tip or with the base [of the finger].
blocks.verse:
अंगुल्यपान्त भागेन छिद्राच्छादः प्रसंशितः।
नात्यग्रेण न मूलेन बंशी छिद्रान् प्रपेरयेत्।७९।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Foreseeing difficulty in sounding the ṛju (plain) notes, and with a mind to touching the śrutis, one should place the fingers [accordingly].
blocks.verse:
ऋजुस्वराणामुच्वारे क्लिष्ताम् परिकल्पयन्।
श्रुतिस्पर्शधिया चैव स्थापये दंगुलीयकान्।८०।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: The practitioner should bear in mind that sometimes, to sound komal notes, even half a hole will have to be opened, and then it may be impossible to bend the finger. The second point is that if, in going from one note to another, touching the śrutis in between — that is, mīṇḍ (glide) — is wanted, then the placement of the fingers can be a hindrance. So, to be saved from troubles that will come in the future, place the fingers correctly right now. For this it is best to set the upāntya (next-to-last) part of the fingers on the holes. Some people bend the long finger for the convenience of the little finger. This is wholly harmful. For clarity, look at the figures.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: One should strike the fingers a hundred times each, one by one; by enduring pain in the limb, the strength of the limb grows.
blocks.verse:
शतम् शतम् समाहन्या दंगुलीयान् पृथक् पृथक्।
अंग पीड़ाम् प्रसहयैव ह्यंग शक्तिः प्रवर्धते।८१।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: In this age of short lives, a special kind of practice for quick success is described in this śloka. Once the placement of the fingers on the flute is well established, each finger should be struck in its place, separately, a hundred times each, so that with unbroken practice pain begins in the finger; and by keeping even the aching finger moving, strength will come quickly to the fingers, just as heating iron quickly makes it pliable. At the same time the mind, busy with counting, also gains concentration. If the fingers of both hands are struck one at a time, by turns, progress can be even faster. In the same way, it will be fitting first to cook the breath, the tongue and the fingers separately for a while, as described above — like rice, dal and vegetables — in the fire of practice with the water of faith added, and then to combine all three and move on to the practice of svara (notes) and laya (tempo). On this, see the śloka —

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: With all the holes covered, the blowing is done very gently; the sound that arises from it is indeed the first.
blocks.verse:
छिद्रान् सर्वान् समाच्छाद्य फूत्कारस्तु शनैः शनैः।
क्रीयते तेन यो नादो जायते प्रथमो हि सः।८२।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: With all the holes in the flute, however many there are, properly closed, the nāda (sound) that comes from blowing very gently — take that as the first note of the flute. Keep in mind that if the holes are not completely closed, the note may change and become the eighth note.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: By lifting the ring finger the second sound is said [to arise]; by lifting the middle finger the third is indeed sounded.
blocks.verse:
अनामिकाम् समुत्थाय द्वितीयो नाद उच्यते।
मध्यमाम् तु समुत्थाप्य तृतीयो नाद्यते खलु।८३।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That is, opening the lowest hole produces the second sound, and opening the second hole the third.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: By lifting the index finger the fourth sound is sounded; then, by lifting the other ring finger, the fifth.
blocks.verse:
तर्जनीं च समुत्थाप्य तूर्यो नादो निनाद्यते।
अथानामिकामन्या मुत्थाप्यैव च पंचमः।८४।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That is, lifting the anāmikā, that is, the third finger, of the other hand produces the pañcama (fifth) note. But keep in mind that, as soon as that finger is lifted, the ring finger of the first hand, which was already raised, should be put back on its own hole. Otherwise, once all the fingers are lifted, the flute will have no support and may fall to the ground.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: By lifting the middle fingers the sixth sound arises. Then, by lifting all of them except the first ring finger,
blocks.verse:
मध्यमांश्च समुत्थाप्य नादः षष्ठ उदीयते।
समुत्थाप्य ततः सर्वान् प्रथमा नामिकाम् विना।८५।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: with the force of the stroke of breath the seventh note is sounded. Then, covering all [the holes], the tāra (upper) [Sa] is sounded.
blocks.verse:
प्राणाधातस्य वेगेन नाद्यते सप्तमः स्वरः।
ततः सर्वान् समाच्छाद्य तार निनाद्यते।८६।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: In the same order, lifting the next finger, that is, the middle finger, produces the sixth sound, that is, dhaivata (Dha), and lifting the last, the index finger, produces the seventh sound, called niṣāda (Ni). But the force of the breath, rising step by step, becomes so great by Ni that if, blowing with that same force, we close all the holes at once, the eighth sound, that is, Ṡa of the tāra (upper) octave, is produced.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: When, with a strong stroke of breath, one sounds the seven in order as before, then there are fourteen sounds.
blocks.verse:
तिव्राधातेन प्राणस्य क्रमसः पूर्व वद्यदा।
सप्तानाम् नादनम् कुर्यात् तदा नादा श्चतुर्दश।८७।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: If in this way one keeps lifting the fingers as before while increasing the strength of the breath, the seven notes of the second octave will be produced. So it is proved that by increasing the force of the breath the same seven sounds have gone into another octave — just as any number, on gaining a zero, changes from units to tens. But by blowing harder still, only two or three notes of the third octave can come out. In this way, in a flute with six holes, usually a total of 15 śuddha (natural) notes are produced, in this order: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni | Ṡa Ṙe Ġa Ṁa Ṗa Ḋha Ṅi | Ṡa. For the remaining komal notes, the method of opening less than half a hole has to be adopted. In a flute with eight holes there are holes for komal Ga and komal Dha as well.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Sa, Ri, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha and Ni: these are held to be the seven notes. Beginning from each one in turn, mūrchanā is practised by the wise.
blocks.verse:
सरी गमौ पधौ निश्चेत्येते सप्तस्वरा मताः।
एकैकस्मात् समारभ्य मूर्छनाऽभ्यस्यते बुधैः।८८।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Although we have seated the seven notes on these holes in order so that it is easy to understand, it is not necessary that the hole we have given the place of 'Ma' should always be 'Ma'. If we take the second hole as 'Sa', the third hole can be 'Re'. In ancient times this procedure was called mūrchanā. It would not be inappropriate if we called it the svara sāriṇi procedure. In the making section of this book I have placed all the notes taking ('Ma') as 'Sa', which is the common practice. Here, for the first practice, the first hole is taken as 'Sa', which later on will be taken as 'Pa'. Then again, now and then, for one's own convenience, any one of the above 7 notes may be taken as 'Sa'.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: See the svara sāriṇi figure below —

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: The practitioner should practise 5 of these mūrchanās a hundred times each. And sometimes practise taking all 16 notes up from bottom to top and down from top to bottom in one breath. But do not forget to increase the force of the breath step by step, and then to reduce it on the way back. In this practice keep the speed only such that no note is lost or skipped over and left out. The speed of the fingers will naturally increase little by little, and the breath too will become long. Only when at least two ārohāvaroha (ascents and descents) in one breath are mastered should you consider yourself qualified to play the flute.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: In each higher sound the blowing should be stronger; and in descending through the sounds there is a gradual lessening of breath.
blocks.verse:
उपर्युपरि नादेषु फूत्कारो बलवान् भवेत्।
अवरोहे तु नादेषु क्रमसः प्राणन्यूनता।८९।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That is, as the sound climbs higher, more force has to be given to the breath, and when the sound begins to come down, in that descending state weakness comes gradually into the breath. But how much should this more-or-less breath be? In this the guru's (teacher's) contribution will be necessary. Otherwise this judgement can go wrong. In the same way, the second necessary point is that —

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: The upper hole is completed by joining with the hole below; therefore, having released the lower one, one should then release the upper.
blocks.verse:
संयुज्या धस्तनाच्छिद्रा दूर्ध्वच्छिद्रं प्रपूर्यते।
तस्मा दधस्तनं मुक्त्वा तत ऊर्ध्व विमोचयेत्।९०।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That is, the note from any hole becomes fully true only when at least two holes below that hole are open and the upper hole gets their proper support. Keeping this in mind, when the practitioner opens the first hole from the bottom, then for its completeness he takes support from the lowest hole, which itself always stays open. So if the lower hole has been closed by some chance object, it must certainly be opened. Now, when you lift the second finger, keep the finger lifted before it raised as well. In the same way, while lifting the third finger, keep the first and second fingers open too. But when you lift the first finger of the other hand, that is, the fourth finger, put the first raised finger back on its hole at the same time. Keep that hole closed until the last, that is, the sixth, hole is open. In this way, up to the last hole, all the holes will keep getting the support of their neighbours too, and the flute will not fall from the hand. Then, coming back, as you close three holes from the top, open the lowest finger, and close all the holes in order from the top.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: There is special effort for practitioners going from one octave to another; so that should be practised separately, again and again.
blocks.verse:
आयासस्तु विशेषः स्यात् सप्तकात् सप्तकेऽपरे।
गच्छताम् साधकानां हि तत्पृथक् साध्यताम् मुहुः।९१।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That is, after opening all the holes, closing them all at once makes the next note come out as 'Sa' of the second octave. To make this difficulty easy, one should raise and lower five fingers from the top together, again and again. Making the procedure of ārohāvaroha (ascent and descent) on the flute still clearer —

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Where the ascent begins, there it should end; let the descent too be made on those same [notes], of eight mātrās (beats).
blocks.verse:
यत आरभ्य आरोहस्तस्मिन्नेव समापनम्।
क्रीयतामचरोहोऽपि तेष्वेवाष्टमात्रिकः।९२।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That is, from whatever note the ascent is made, taking it as 'Sa', end the eighth note, after seven notes, on that same hole. And then, descending from that same note, the eighth count will come back to its earlier place. In this way an ascent of eight mātrās (beats) and a descent of eight mātrās, 16 mātrās in all, will take this form: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni Ṡa, Ṡa Ni Dha Pa Ma Ga Re Sa. By chanting this root mantra of 18 mātrās at least 100 times and at most 1000 times every day, siddhis (accomplishments) are attained. Sometimes, while reciting the 16 mātrās aloud, count them in order with the help of the fingers, as follows —

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: On each finger one should make four parts, and take those parts in order with the tip of the thumb.
blocks.verse:
अंगुलीयक एकस्मिन् कूर्याद् भागचतुष्टयम्।
अंगुष्ठाग्रेण गृहणीयात् तांश्च भागान् क्रमेण वै।९३।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Then on the other fingers one should count in order as before; thus there will be sixteen mātrās (beats) on the four fingers.
blocks.verse:
ततः परांगुलीयेषु गणयेत् पूर्ववत् क्रमात्।
तेन षोड़श मात्राः स्यूरंगुलीय चतुष्टयें।९४।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That is, if you count by taking each finger as four parts and placing the tip of the thumb on those parts in order, you can easily count up to 16 mātrās (beats).

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Just as any flowing river has four directions, so practice too stays alive in four ways: sunanā, cunanā, gunanā and dhunanā — śravaṇa (listening), cayana (choosing), gunana (pondering) and upayoga (use). If you listen to any song or tune with concentration, then pick out from it a few things that matter to you, then sit alone and hum it, and then keep using it at the right time, any practice will keep blossoming and putting out leaves, and will keep flowing along with life. Now some methods of practising the notes with laya (tempo) are presented.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Keeping all the notes in mind, one should play them properly again and again; one should make the speed less or more, gradually, according to one's strength.
blocks.verse:
अनुध्याय स्वरान् सर्वान् विधिना वादयेन्मुहुः।
गतिं न्यूनाधिकमं कूर्याद् यथाशक्ति शनैः शनैः।९५।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: While doing the ārohāvaroha (ascent and descent) of the notes, the player should also keep in mind the names of those notes, so that, if asked suddenly, he can quickly play any note and show it. Just as children learning multiplication tables want to repeat from the beginning to answer any question, the same thing happens to those practitioners.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: The second suggestion is that if, while playing the ārohāvaroha (ascent and descent), its speed increases, let it increase only so far that the purity of the notes is not spoiled.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: The third suggestion is that, while increasing the speed, when some errors appear, correct them at that same speed; then, when you feel unable, reduce that speed little by little.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: The fourth point is this: if you take the form of ārohāvaroha (ascent and descent) made in this order — (Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni Ṡa Ṙe Ṡa Ni Dha Pa Ma Ga Re Sa) (ṭa ka ṭa ka ṭa ka ṭa ka ṭa ka ṭa ka ka ṭa ṭa ka) — as a great mantra, and chant it attentively at least a hundred times with mental counting, then along with the fingers, the tongue and the breath, the mind too is trained, and through this practice many kinds of siddhis (accomplishments) are attained. The practitioner can see this for himself through his faith; this secret is not fit to be written.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Now the method of practising the notes with tāla (metric cycle) is presented.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Practice of the notes joined with tāla (metric cycle) bears great fruit; then, dividing time into equal parts, the notes should be practised again and again.
blocks.verse:
अभ्यासस्तालयोगेन स्वराणाम् हि महाफलः।
कालं समं विभाज्याथ स्वराः साध्या मुहुर्मुहुः।९६।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Before practising the notes with tāla (metric cycle), it is necessary to practise the laya (tempo) connected with tāla. The regular movement of anything is called laya. Just as the hand of a clock ticks at regular moments, so if the clap of our hand goes at regular times, we call it laya. Now if we count along with that clap, it will be called a laya of counting equal to the clap.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: For example

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: 1 2 3 4 tā tā tā tā

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: And if we divide the moment of each clap into two equal parts and say two counts in each clap, the laya (tempo) of the counting will be twice that of the clap, for example —

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 tā tā tā tā

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: In the same way, if the moment of the clap is divided into three or four equal parts and as many counts are said, the laya (tempo) of that counting will be called threefold or fourfold. Now if sargam is said in place of the counting, the sargam too will be said to have the same kind of laya. For example —

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: tālī (clap) tālī tālī tālī Equal to the clap Sa Re Ga Ma Double laya SaRe GaMa PaDha NiṠa Triple laya SaReGa MaPaDha NiṠaṠa NiDhaPa Quadruple laya SaReGaMa PaDhaNiṠa ṠaNiDhaPa MaGaReSa

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: In the way shown above, while clapping with the hands, one should recite the sargam with the mouth in different layas (tempos). Keep in mind that while doing double [speed] with the mouth, the speed of the hand does not also start to increase. Then, by marking the clap with the foot, the ability to play the sargam on the flute too will develop. Just as a capable witness (a guru) is needed for knowledge of svara, so a witness is needed for knowledge of laya too, one who can turn the incorrect into correct. Now pay attention to the three states of the notes —

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: There, the wise speak of four varṇas (kinds of melodic movement): sthāyī (steady), ārohī (ascending), avarohī (descending) and sañcārī (wandering), in that order.
blocks.verse:
तत्र वर्णाश्च चत्वारः कथ्यन्ते हि मनीषिभिः।
स्थाय्यारोह्यवरोही च संचारीति यथाक्रमाः।९७।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Just as the four states of stability, rise, decline and busyness give a person many forms and titles, so in the notes, on the basis of the actions of steadiness, climbing, descending and moving about, various groups of notes and tunes arise. A group that is bound to tāla (metric cycle) is called a dhun (tune) or gīt (song). A group that is small and bound only to laya (tempo) we call an alaṅkāra (patterned exercise). Now, there are many texts for the definition of laya and tāla, so after giving a brief introduction to them we will move on to alaṅkāra.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That time which is regulated by strokes is called laya (tempo); and [laya] with a measured number of strokes, divided by empty [beats], is tāla (metric cycle).
blocks.verse:
लयः स कथ्यते कालः यस्त्वाघातैर्नियन्त्रितः।
मिताघातस्तु तालः स्यात् सून्य विभाजितः।९८।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That is, when we regulate the flow of time with regular strokes, that very time is given the name laya (tempo). And when we limit those strokes to a fixed number and divide them with khālī (empty) claps, it is called tāla (metric cycle). Laya is essential in every tāla, but tāla is not necessary in every laya. If laya is the flower, tāla is the garland made of them.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Joining another [note], in order, at the beginning, the end and the middle of the base [note] is called sparśa in the world; it has twelve kinds.
blocks.verse:
मूलाद्यन्तेषु मध्येषु क्रमादन्यस्य योजनम्।
स्पर्ष इत्युच्यते लोके तस्य भेदास्तु द्वादश।९९।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: That is, when one note is given prominence and, taking it as the mūla svara (base note), other notes are combined with it in a special way, it begins to take many forms, like conjunct letters. Learned musicians call this action sparśa (touch) or kaṇa (grace note). Mostly the notes that join with a note are its neighbours on either side. If their various forms are counted, there are mainly 12 kinds. Though more than 12 can also be made.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: 1 - Pūrvādisparśa: if the note before a note is joined at the beginning of the base note, we will call it pūrvādisparśa. For example, the note before 'Ga' is 'Re'; if it is joined at the beginning of the base note, that is, 'Ga', it will be sounded like this: 'Re Ga - -'.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: 2 - Pūrvamadhyasparśa: if we put that same 'Re' in the middle of 'Ga', then, dividing the time of sounding 'Ga' into four equal parts, 'Re' has to be placed between the first part and the third part, that is, in the second part. Its example will be like this: 'Ga Re Ga -'.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: 3 - Pūrvāntasparśa: now if 'Re' is joined in the fourth time-division of 'Ga', we will call it pūrvāntasparśa. It can be sounded like this: 'Ga - - Re'. If this is used in movement, this same end-touch begins to seem like the beginning-touch of the next base note.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: 4 - Parādisparśa: in the same way, the note 'Ma', which follows 'Ga', that is, comes after it, can be joined at the three places in turn.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: 5 - Paramadhyasparśa: joining [it] at the beginning, the middle and the end of the base note 'Ga',

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: 6 - Parāntasparśa: there can be three kinds, 'MaGa--', 'GaMaGa-' and 'Ga--Ma', whose names are written in order.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: 7 - Pūrvādyubhayasparśa: if the preceding and the following [notes] are joined to the base note together, there can be conjunct forms such as 'ReMaGa-'.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: 8 - But if its order is reversed, we will call it parādyubhayasparśa. In sounding, their form will be like this: 'ReMaGa-' and 'MaReGa-'.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: 9 - Pūrvādi samūlasparśa, and

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: 10 - Parādi samūlasparśa; their example: ReGaMaGa--- MaGaReGa---

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Then if these are also begun with the [base] note, two more are formed.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: 11 - Mūlādyanekasparśa: 'Ga Re Ga Ma Ga-'. These very groups of many joined notes are also called mirkī or murkī.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: 12 - In this way the glory of the sparśas, taking its endless forms in svaraśāstra (the science of notes), spreads from classical music to folk music. These were the touches of notes on a note; now the touch of śrutis on the notes, which the learned call mīṇḍ (glide), is considered.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Two methods of ascent and descent are described with thought; the movement in them is, separately, like that of the snake and of the frog.
blocks.verse:
आरोहस्यावरोहस्य द्वे विधी वर्णिते धिया।
अहि मन्डूक वच्चैव गतिस्तत्र पृथक् पृथक्।१००।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Wherever there is a question of climbing or descending, two kinds of method are possible: one sliding like a snake, and the other jumping like a frog. On this basis people build steps in their houses for climbing with the feet, and also build a separate slope for taking a bicycle up. If on the flute a long, channel-like hole were made from one hole to another, and one went from the first to the second note by sliding with some smooth metal, this would be called śrutisparśa (touching the śrutis) ascent or descent, because the sounds lying between the first hole, Sa, and the second hole, Re — which we call śrutis — are touched. To master this difficult action, flute players practise not only lifting the fingers but also lacāva (flexing) them. When you raise and set the finger on the hole many times while flexing it, the action of mīṇḍ (glide) will begin to happen. Flex it in whatever direction suits you, so that the hole opens slowly and closes slowly. If one note is far from the other, as in 'Sa Ma', flex the fingers together at the same time, so that the flexing is not broken anywhere.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: On one note there is kampana (shake); on two notes, vaiparītya (reversal); on three notes there is laṅgha (leap); and on four, sañcāra (movement).
blocks.verse:
कम्पनम् स्वर एकस्मिन् वैपरीत्यं स्वरद्वये।
स्वरत्रते तु लंघः स्यात् संचारस्तु चतुष्टये।१०१।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Just as in a field of work one person alone can do only a little work, two people together more than that, three together more than that, and four people together accomplish many kinds of tasks — in the same way, making clear which elements grow, when [notes] are used in rāgas, from one note up to four notes, the śloka above has told that as long as any note stays alone, no action other than kampana (shake) can happen in it, as if that note were trembling, frightened of loneliness. But as soon as it meets one other note, many activities begin between the two of them: ādisparśa (touch at the beginning), antasparśa (touch at the end), turning back and forth, and so on. Seen in a worldly way, it seems as if the two have become so absorbed in each other that a third note will have to come to bring them to their senses.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: Now when the third also comes and joins, then among those three notes, besides the earlier actions, a new action in the form of laṅghana (leaping) begins, as if the third were now and then making a disturbance between the two notes. After that, when four notes come together, along with the growth of the earlier actions a new action, saṃvāda (dialogue), begins, as if all could become calm and happy. The gradation of qualities grows only up to four notes, so in practice the sargam is what is well known. The actions of different notes among the notes, which come from the mixing of the qualities written above, have been given the name varṇa. So it is from the actions that the varṇa, that is, the class (jāti), is decided.

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: There, the wise speak of four varṇas (kinds of melodic movement): sthāyī (steady), ārohī (ascending), avarohī (descending) and sañcārī (wandering), in that order.
blocks.verse:
तत्र वर्णाश्च चत्वारः कथ्यन्ते हि मनीषिभिः।
सथाय्यारोद्यवरोही च संचारीति यथा क्रमः।१०२।

blocks.subsection_title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
blocks.text: In this way these same [actions] have been named the four classes (jātis) of varṇa: sthāyī (steady), ārohī (ascending), avarohī (descending) and sañcārī (wandering). But to make alaṅkāras (patterned exercises), we have to look at those elements of the notes on whose basis alaṅkāras can be made as needed. So, on the basis of the qualities described above, examples of alaṅkāras are presented.
Definition of alaṅkāra
When, in ascent and descent, a particular arrangement of order [among the notes] is made, and it is sounded joined with laya (tempo), that alone is called alaṅkāra (patterned exercise).
blocks.verse:
यदाऽरोहेऽवरोहे च विशिष्ट क्रमयोजना।
उच्चारो लययोगेन सैवालंकार उच्यते।१०३।

blocks.text: That is, when a particular order is arranged among the notes, and ascent and so on are performed with it based on laya (tempo), it is called alaṅkāra (patterned exercise). But bear in mind that an order formed in two or three notes should be carried through the whole ascent and descent. For example, 'Sa Re Ga' and 'Sa Ga Re': both these note groups are made of only three notes, but if the order of the first is 1, 2, 3, then the order of the second is 1, 3, 2. If we carry the first of these orders through 'Re Ga Ma' instead of 'Sa Re Ga', and then through the other notes, the following alaṅkāra will be formed - Sa Re Ga, Re Ga Ma, Ga Ma Pa, Ma Pa Dha, Pa Dha Ni, Dha Ni Ṡa | Ṡa Ni Dha, Ni Dha Pa, Dha Pa Ma, Pa Ma Ga, Ma Ga Re, Ga Re Sa. And by carrying the second order through the other notes - Sa Ga Re, Re Ma Ga, Ga Pa Ma, Ma Dha Pa, Pa Ni Dha, Dha Ṡa Ni | Ṡa Dha Ni, Ni Pa Dha, Dha Ma Pa, Pa Ga Ma, Ma Re Ga, Ga Sa Re - this alaṅkāra will arise.
In alaṅkāras, besides the particular order, there are other subtle elements too.
The inclusion of laya (tempo) and tāla (metric cycle), the imitation of words (śabdānukaraṇa), and the development of the power of the notes (svara-śakti): these are the qualities born of alaṅkāra.
blocks.verse:
लय ताल समावेशः शब्दानुकरणं तथा।
स्वर शक्ति विकाशश्चे त्येतेऽलंकारजा गुणाः।१०४।

blocks.text: As soon as alaṅkāra (patterned exercise) is discussed, three questions arise in the mind: (1) In how many notes is this alaṅkāra arranged? (2) Of how many mātrās (beats) is this order? (3) What is its special feature with regard to cāl (movement)? It is these very questions that are being answered.

The inclusion of laya (tempo) and tāla (metric cycle) in any alaṅkāra, the imitation of words, and the development of the svara-śaktis (powers of the notes) as befits an alaṅkāra, are given below; they resemble the actions described earlier.
Āvṛtti (repetition) is in one note; vaiparītya (reversal) in two notes; in three notes there is laṅgha (leaping); and sañcāra (movement) in four.
blocks.verse:
आवृत्तिस्तु स्वरैके स्वयाद् वैपरीत्यं स्वरद्वये।
स्वरत्रये भवेल्लंघः संचारस्तु चतुष्टये।१०५।

blocks.text: Āvṛtti (repetition) means repeating a note again and again. But if a group of two or three notes is repeated, understand it as dvayāvṛtti (two-note repetition) and trayāvṛtti (three-note repetition) respectively.
Kinds of āvṛtti (repetition) Ekāvṛtti (one-note repetition) Dvayāvṛtti (two-note repetition) Trayāvṛtti (three-note repetition) Sa Sa Sa SaRe SaRe SaReGa SaReGa

This is a simple quality, which is ordinarily possible in anything from one note to many notes. But repetition of more than three is impractical. A somewhat more precious quality lies in two notes: vaiparītya (reversal), that is, being turned over, and being smaller and larger. This quality is impossible in one note, just as, if someone has only one son, it is impossible to decide whether he is the younger or the elder. More precious still is the quality that lives in three notes, or in more than three notes: laṅghita (leaping), that is, leaving out some note in between and going on to a note further ahead. For example, 'Sa Ga'.

Better still is the quality that lives in four notes: (sañcāra) wandering. All the qualities above are possible in many alaṅkāras (patterned exercises); even so, in a given alaṅkāra one quality is found to predominate. For example -

In the same way, on the basis of just three notes, alaṅkāras (patterned exercises) can be made from Dādarā up to Tīntāl, that is, from six mātrās (beats) to 16 mātrās. Making orders of notes according to the short and long syllables in words is called śabdānukaraṇa (imitation of words). If someone spoke a word (paṅkaja), we should understand it as paṃ - ka ja, because uttering paṃ takes more time than 'ka' and 'ja'. Following it, [the notes] will be Sa - Re Ga. Now more examples are presented.

Men, women and gods are all adorned with alaṅkāras (ornaments); by alaṅkāras indeed the worlds, the notes and poems are made beautiful.
blocks.verse:
नरा नार्यश्च देवाश्च सर्वेऽलंकार भूषिताः।
अलंकारैर्हि लोकाश्च स्वराः काव्याश्च शोभिताः।१०६।

blocks.text: That is, the real meaning of alaṅkāra is a means of decoration, that is, an ornament. From Prakṛti (nature) to Puruṣa, all are its takers. In this world men, women, gods, demons, poetry and music: all these honour alaṅkāra.

In the world of musical notes, indeed, nothing works without alaṅkāra. The three states of alaṅkāra are scientific. (1) When the sādhaka (practitioner) arranges certain fixed notes in a particular order and then keeps carrying that order regularly through the following notes, he begins to sense the truth of that order; this state is called sādhyāvasthā (the state of striving). (2) When the sādhaka, absorbed in its unbroken japa (repetition), begins to experience concentration and peace in the mind, this is called the siddhāvasthā (state of attainment) of that alaṅkāra. And when the sādhaka uses it effortlessly in some song or the like, then, in the form of a mirkī (quick turn of notes), it delights people and touches the heart. This third state is called rasapradā (giving rasa). It would be apt if we take these three states as examples of satyam, śivam and sundaram (the true, the good and the beautiful). This is the meaning of the following śloka.
They have three states: sādhyā (to be attained), siddhā (attained) and rasapradā (giving rasa). The first [two belong] to vistāra (elaboration) and tānas, and the rasapradā to songs.
blocks.verse:
तिस्रोऽवस्थाश्च तेषां स्युः साध्या सिद्धा रसप्रदा।
आद्ये विस्तारतानेषु गीतेषु च रसप्रदा।१०६।

blocks.text: If alaṅkāras (patterned exercises) are composed in three notes by the rule of mathematics, using only ekāvṛtti (one-note repetition) with the help of laṅghana (skipping), the following 36 alaṅkāras can be composed.
SaReGaGa SaSaReGa SaReReGa SaGaReGa SaReSaGa - from Sa to Ga --- 5+
SaGaReRe SaSaGaRe SaGaGaRe SaReGaRe SaGaSaRe - from Sa to Re --- 5+
SaReGaSa SaGaReSa - from Sa to Sa -- 2 = 12
In the same way, beginning from Re and from Ga, there will be 12*3=36 in all.
Now, the elements of tāna

When I have to build tānas (fast melodic runs) in a particular rāga, I have to maintain the qualities of the rāga and their jātis (classes by number of notes). In such a situation it is difficult to carry through alaṅkāras (patterned exercises). To get over this difficulty, [we] attend to the subtle elements within the alaṅkāras, and carry those same elements through in the tānas.

Laṅgha (skipping), nivarta (turning back), bārdhakya (gradual expansion), pakṣaika-paripakvatā (strengthening one side), rāga-vācaka-puṣṭi (reinforcing the rāga's identifying phrase), and gamakas (ornamental oscillations), held to be of various kinds;
blocks.verse:
लंघो निर्वर्तो बार्धक्यं पक्षैक परिपक्वता।
राग वाचक पुष्टिश्च गमकाश्च विविधास्मृताः।१०८।

blocks.text: anyārambha (beginning on a different note), samāpti (ending [on a different note]), likewise the mixing of layas (tempos), vakratā (crooked movement) and āvṛttis (repetitions): these are held to be the eleven qualities.
blocks.verse:
अन्यारम्भः समाप्तिश्च लयानाम् मिश्रणं तथा।
वक्रताऽ वृत्तयश्चैते गुणा स्त्वेकादशस्मृताः।१०९।

blocks.text: That is, from a practical point of view there are eleven main qualities used in tānas (fast melodic runs). And by mixing any two or three of these, many more qualities can arise; all of them are tāna-tattvas (elements of tāna). These qualities are described below with examples.
1 - Laṅghana (skipping)
Laṅghana (skipping) is used in ascent or descent in two ways. One is on its own, as in (Sa Ga Re Ma Ga Pa); the other mixed with alaṅghana (not skipping), as in (SaRe SaGa ReGa ReMa)
2 - Nivartana (turning back)

The literal meaning of nivartana is 'returning'. When, before the ascent is completed, some part of the descent is mixed in and then the ascent is made again, this action is called nivartana (turning back). For example (Sa Re Ga Re Sa Re Ga Ga)
3 - (Bārdhakya) Baṛhat (gradual expansion)

In this action too nivartana (turning back) is necessary, but in it one has to return again and again to a fixed place and then advance regularly one note at a time; so it has an existence somewhat different from nivartana. For example - (Sa Re Sa, Sa Re Ga Re Sa, Sa Re Ga Ma Ga Re Sa, Sa Re GaMa Ma Pa Ma Ga Re Sa). In this way the group of notes keeps growing, step after step.
4 - Pakṣaika paripakvatā (strengthening one side)

It means strengthening one of the two sides, ascent or descent, in many ways. It is a more suitable action mostly for rāgas of the auḍava-sampūrṇa jāti (five notes in ascent, all seven in descent), as in Bihāg - ( Ga Re Sa, Ma Ga Re Sa, Pa Ma′ Ga Ma Ga Re Sa, Ni Dha Pa Ma Ga Re Sa)
5 - Rāga-vācaka puṣṭi (reinforcing the rāga's identifying phrase)

That is, presenting the group of notes by which the rāga becomes clearer, beginning it from different notes. This action is mostly used in saṅkīrṇa (mixed) rāgas. For example - to keep Rāmkalī apart from Bhairav -- Ma′ Pa komal Dha komal Ni komal Dha Pa komal Re Ga Ma Pa Ma′ Pa komal Dha komal Ni komal Dha Pa, Ṡa Ni komal Dha! Pa Ma′ Pa komal Dha komal Ni komal Dha Pa Ma Pa Ga Ma Ga komal Re Sa. Or, in a song, bringing out any one of these four aspects, words, sargam, notes and tāla (metric cycle), is also an example of it.
6 - Gamaka

This is a celebrated action, whose description is given in other treatises too. My view does not differ from theirs. (svarasya kampo gamakaḥ) That is, the use of shaken notes is called gamaka (ornamental oscillation). Performers use various kinds of gamaka with their skill, which are impossible to write down; but the ordinary gamaka, in which the sparśa (touch) note predominates, is like this: ( Sa Re SaGa ReGa Re Sa Re Ga ReMa GaMa Ga Re Sa). If the sparśa note is taken out of this, it will become merely an example of ekāvṛtti (one-note repetition).
7 - Anyārambha (beginning on a different note)
Its meaning is to begin from one note after another and end on one [note], for example - (in Yaman - Ṇi Re Ga, ḌhaṆi Re Ga, Ma′ Ga Re Ga, Ni Dha Pa Ma′ Ga Re Ga)
8 - Anya samāpti (ending on a different note)
Beginning from one note and ending on other notes, changing each time. For example - in Yaman Ṇi Re Ga, Ṇi Re Ga Ma′ Pa, Ṇi Re Ma′ Dha Ni, Ni Dha Pa Ma′ Ga Re Sa).
9 - Layānām miśraṇam (mixing tempos)

When a tāna (fast melodic run) is flowing in one laya (tempo) and suddenly, leaving that laya, its double or half laya is mixed in momentarily, again and again, we may call this action miśralaya (mixed tempo). Only accomplished sādhakas (practitioners) can do this. In it, the blending of many layas is more interesting, as, in Rāga Yaman itself - Ṇi ReRe Ga Ma′ - DhaPa Ma′ Ga Ma′ Ma′Dha -Dha Ni Dha NiNi Dha Pa - DhaDha Pa Ma′ Ga -- Ma′Ma′ Dha Ni Ṡa NiDha Pa Ma′Ga ReGa -Re Sa.
10 - Vakratā (crooked movement)

This action is useful for vakra (crooked) rāgas. For example GaRe MaGa PaMa′ DhaPa Ma′ Ga PaRe Sa, Ma′ Ga PaMa′ DhaPa NiDha Ṡa, and so on. 'In rāgas such as Gauṛ Sāraṅg - MaGa PaMa′ DhaPa Ma′Ga PaRe Sa. MaGa PaMa′ DhaPa NiDha Ṡa
11 - Āvṛtti (repetition)

It is mainly of three kinds, as in GaGa ReRe SaSa NiNiNi Re Re Re Ga. This we call ekāvṛtti (one-note repetition). And ṠaNiDha ṠaNiDha PaMa′Ga PaMa′Ga - this we call trayāvṛtti (three-note repetition). Repetition of more notes than this can indeed be done, but in practice it is not suitable from the point of view of beauty.

Besides the above 11 actions there are some more actions too, such as 'miśra saptaka' (mixed octave), that is, saying the same group of notes in two octaves, as in Ga Re Sa, Ġa Ṙe Ṡa. But for fear of enlarging the book, more actions are not being mentioned.
Having set up two notes, or three, or four, one should form a samudāya (group of notes) in an order of one's own devising.
blocks.verse:
स्वरद्वयम् प्रकल्प्याथ त्रयम् वा तु चतुष्टयम्।
स्वकल्पित क्रमेणैव समुदायम् प्रकल्पयेत्।११०।

blocks.text: That is, taking two notes, or more, three or four notes, and carrying through the elements above in them, the sādhaka (practitioner) should compose samudāyas (groups of notes) of various orders on the basis of his own imagination.
When that order is carried through everywhere, in groups of equal mātrās (beats), then [there is] the making of an alaṅkāra (patterned exercise).
blocks.verse:
तस्य क्रमस्य निर्वाहो यदा सर्वत्र क्रीयते।
समात्रिक समूहेषु तदाऽलंकार कल्पना।१११।

blocks.text: That is, if the order stated before is carried through, step by step, in the following notes, and those mātrās (beats) are also kept in mind, the alaṅkāra (patterned exercise) extends into a full ascending and descending form.

The point is that in the sādhanā (practice) of alaṅkāra one has to keep two kinds of order in mind - one is the order which you have made in two or three notes; the other is the general order of ascent and descent, which is fixed by the śāstra according to the rāga or thāṭ (parent scale). Suppose you composed this order "Sa Re Ga Re Sa" in three notes, which is in five mātrās (beats). If you carry this same order through Re Ga Ma in place of Sa Re Ga, then in place of Sa there will be Re, in place of Re Ga, and in place of Ga Ma, and the second link has formed like this: Re Ga Ma Ga Re. In the same way keep shifting each note forward until it ends on the Ṡa of the tāra saptaka (upper octave). Then, to come back from there, the same order has to be changed into its descending state. That is, the place that Re has in the ascent, Ni will have that same place in the descent. In this way the descending form of Sa Re Ga Re Sa will be Ṡa Ni Dha Ni Ṡa. Now if we want to play its full extension, we should first write it out as below and then play it. Doing so, we can gain an easy flow even in difficult alaṅkāras.

Vārtālāpa (conversation) belongs to language; vilāpa (lament) is in weeping; saṃlāpa (dialogue) is in acting and the like; and likewise ālāpa is in notes.
blocks.verse:
वार्तालापस्तु भाषायाम् विलापो रोदने भवेत्।
संलापोऽभिनयादौ स्यात्तथाऽलापः स्वरेषु च।११२।

blocks.text: Bhāva (feeling) has existed ever since this world was created. Or say that creation itself is full of bhāva, and pralaya (dissolution) is its absence (abhāva). It became necessary for living beings to exchange feelings with one another. It is from just there that we must take the various languages and gestures to have arisen. Along with languages, nāda (sound), and along with gestures, laya (rhythm) arose naturally. When one being began to wish to nurture another, from then on lāpana (speaking) also became necessary. According to the grammar of Śrī Pāṇini, from the root pal comes lāp or pālana (nurturing), and from the root lap comes lāp or lāpana (speaking); these two roots became each other's avaroha (reversal). In the śloka above, the meanings of the root lap with prefixes, and their fields, are shown. If vārtālāpa (conversation) is suited to language, then in the same way vilāpa (lament) is suited to weeping, saṃlāpa (dialogue) to acting, and in the same way ālāpa to notes.
For the dealings of beings living in the world with one another, these were devised by Brahmā as the means of expressing bhāva (feeling).
blocks.verse:
संसारस्थित जीवानाम् व्यवहाराय परस्परम्।
कल्पिता ब्रम्हणा ह्येते भावाभिव्याक्ति हेतवः।११३।

blocks.text: That is, so that the beings in the world can deal with one another, Brahmā himself, through the Sāma Veda, created ālāpa and the like relating to music.

That is, each note has a particular relationship with another note. We may call it bhāva (feeling), and from the union of the bhāvas of several notes arises a rāga full of bhāva, which is delightful or rasa-enhancing for all beings in the world.
The note called ṣaḍja is held to be the begetter of the six [other] notes. By it alone is the bhāva (feeling) completed, as [the sense of] words is by the verb.
blocks.verse:
षण्णाम् स्वराणाम् जनकः षड्जाख्यः खरो मतः।
तेनैव भावस्य पूर्तिः स्याच्छब्दानाम् क्रियया यथा।११५।

blocks.text: When we accept some nāda (sound) as Sa, then the remaining notes have to be fixed on its basis. So the full name of Sa has been given as ṣaḍja, that is, the one that gives birth to the six. Just as in any language the sense of the other words depends on the verb, in the same way in music too the sense of all the notes is completed only on Sa. If one does not rest on Sa, the ālāpa will seem meaningless. Understood roughly, ālāpa or svara-vistāra (elaboration of notes) rests on just three main actions: movement in some notes, rest on some notes, and the full stop on Sa. Just as in conversation many pauses are expected, from the comma to the full stop, in the same way in ālāpa too there are four kinds of pause: nyāsa, apanyāsa, vinyāsa and sanyāsa. Human life too is furnished with movement and pauses. Although man projects only the bhāva (feeling) in his heart onto notes and tāla, and, seeing life as ascent, descent and sthāī (steady state), sees his own bhāva reflected in the mirror of the notes, still it is a practical truth that going from Sa to komal Re gives the feeling of karuṇa rasa (pathos), and going to śuddha Re gives the feeling of śānta rasa (calm). And on returning to Sa again, that feeling becomes more vivid, as it were, and makes its impression on the listeners. So the effect of all the notes is held to arise from Sa alone: the nearer a note is to Sa, the more bhāva it can bring out, and the effect of a note far from Sa grows faint. So to keep that effect fresh, Pañcama and Madhyama make the contribution of Sa itself. This is the meaning of the following śloka.
For the feelings of notes placed far away to be experienced, Pañcama is the helper; in its absence, the note Madhyama.
blocks.verse:
दूरवर्ति स्वरस्थानाम् भावानामनु भुतये।
पंचमस्तु सहायः स्यादभावे मध्यमः स्वरः।११६।

blocks.text: When we want to do svara-vistāra (elaboration of notes) or ālāpa in a rāga, it is first of all necessary for us to know the separate importance of the notes used in that rāga. Generally the importance of Sa is the same in all rāgas. It will be quite fitting if we regard it as the Mahārājā of the kingdom that is the rāga. After it, the second place has to be given to Pañcama, because it is Sa's helper, in the role of Prime Minister. If Pañcama is varjit (omitted) in that rāga, then in its absence Madhyama is accepted. After that, the vādī (principal note) and saṃvādī (consonant second note) of that rāga we can liken to the Governor and the Chief Minister. Then we give the other notes the place of ordinary subjects. Once such an arrangement is made, moving on the ordinary notes and stopping on the special notes: these are the only two actions we have to do. In moving, the use of tāna elements, and in stopping, a beautiful kampan (shake), will be graceful. In the ālāpa of a rāga my attitude will be that of a curious tourist in a particular city. That is, fixing one place for the night's stay, setting out each day for one important place, and coming back again to the fixed place. If on the way one has to stop a little for some special reason, one must stop only for a short time and keep one's destination in mind. At the destination, walking around and sitting in due manner will come naturally. If some things are left unseen at that place, one can set out for the same place again the next day too. So it is proved that pauses can be made in many ways.
Two other notes standing here in the relation of ṣaḍja and pañcama would be the vādī and saṃvādī, which shape [and set apart] the form of the rāga.
blocks.verse:
षड्ज पञ्चम भावेन स्थितावन्यौ स्वराविह।
वादि संवादिनौ स्याताम् रागरूप विवर्तकौ।११७।

blocks.text: That is, the two notes between which the ṣaḍja-pañcama relation exists are held to be the vādī (principal note) and saṃvādī (consonant second note) of one rāga or another. And by these alone being changed, rāgas with the same notes are also understood as different; for example, in Rāga Bhūpālī Ga and Dha are vādī and saṃvādī, and in Rāga Deśkār Dha is vādī and Ga saṃvādī.
Nyāsa, apanyāsa, vinyāsa and sanyāsa are the pauses, through which the greater or lesser importance of the notes comes about.
blocks.verse:
न्यासापन्यास विन्यास सन्यासास्तु विरामकाः।
न्यूनाधिकम् महत्वं तु स्वराणां यैस्तु संभवः।११८।

blocks.text: On the notes of greater or lesser importance in rāgas we use four kinds of pause. First, we play many note groups ending on the vādī (principal) note, one after another, and in each of those note groups we make an ordinary pause; this we call nyāsa (resting note). The slight short pause that we make on some other note in order to complete that nyāsa, we call upanyāsa. If within the nyāsa we utter a particular note group again and again and reinforce it in many ways, we call these pauses vinyāsa (varied rest), because variety and distinctiveness are both expressed by the prefix 'vi'. And when, after these nyāsas, we come to Sa and feel rest, this is called sanyāsa (final rest on Sa). For example, in Rāga Yaman, on the note Gāndhāra: Ni Re Ga, PaMa′ Ga, Re Ma′ Ga - these are nyāsas. And NiRe Ga ReGa Ma′ PaMa′ Ga, Ṇi Ḍha Ṇi Re Ma′ Ga, Ṇi Ṇi Re - Ṇi Ṇi Ga - - these are all vinyāsas endowed with the qualities of alaṅkāra; and ṆiRe GaMa′ Pa -- PaMa′ Ga: here, after making apanyāsa on Pañcama, the nyāsa of Ga took place. Then Ga Re -- ṆiRe Sa. Here, after making apanyāsa on Re, sanyāsa was made on Sa.
Āndolana (oscillation), vakratva (crookedness), abhyāsa (repetition), svara-saṅgati (association of notes) and vikarṣaṇa (pulling) of the śrutis: these are held to be the five actions.
blocks.verse:
आंदोलन च वक्रत्वं अभ्यासः स्वर संगति।
विकर्षणं श्रुतीनां चेत्येते पंच किृया मताः।११९।

blocks.text: In the svara-vistāra (elaboration of notes) of rāgas, five actions are done besides the tāna elements. Their names are given in the śloka above. 1 Āndolana (oscillation), that is, making the blowing breath tremble on the note on which one pauses. This āndolana is mostly done on the guitar. On the bansī (bamboo flute) some people are not able to do it, because for that it is necessary for the sādhaka (practitioner) to practise bhastrikā prāṇāyāma (breath control) for 6 months in the winters. When we take the breath in and out quickly, just as a dog sits and pants in the hot days, that kind of practice is called bhastrikā prāṇāyāma. It should be done for two or three minutes every day. 2 Vakratva (crookedness): when we do not sound a note straight, but use it joined with the notes around it, we show a changed form, sometimes with one sparśa (touch) and sometimes with many sparśas, that is, in the form of mirkīs - this we call a saṃyukta svara (joined note) or vakra svara (crooked note). In other śāstras there is a somewhat different definition of vakra, but by that the crookedness of the rāga becomes clear, not that of the note. 3 Abhyāsa (repetition) means repeating the rāga-identifying note group. 4 Vikarṣaṇa (pulling) means drawing the śrutis in between, in the form of mīṇḍ (glide), to go from one note to another. 5 Svara-saṅgati (association of notes) means using, besides the vādī and saṃvādī, the association of some [other] notes that suits the rāga.
Placing vinyāsa many times on the vādī, after apanyāsa on the secondary [notes], one should make sanyāsa on ṣaḍja; then rāga-ālāpa comes about.
blocks.verse:
बहुधा बादिनि विन्यस्य गौणेऽपन्यास पूर्वकम्।
सन्यासः षड्जे कूर्याद्रागालापस्तदा भवेत्।१२०।

blocks.text: That is, after making apanyāsa (intermediate resting note) on the gauṇa (anuvādī, assonant) notes, making vinyāsa in many ways on the vādī (principal) note, and making sanyāsa on Sa: this is the meaning of rāgālāpa. Here it is necessary to show, with an example, the signs for nyāsa and the others.

The sign of ordinary nyāsa will be given as (+), in the form of a plus; the sign of vinyāsa as (,); the sign of apanyāsa as (-), in the form of a khaṇḍākār (fragment); and the sign of sanyāsa as (||), in the form of a full stop.
Some ālāpas of Rāga Yaman
(1) Ṇi Re Ga + Ṇi Re Ga Ma′ Re Ga + Ṇi Re Ma′ – Ma′ Ga, Ṇi Re Re Ma′ Ga, Pa Ma′ Ga Re Ga, Ṇi Re Ga Ma′ Pa – Re Ga, Ga Re – Ga Re Ṇi Re – Sa|
(2) Ṇi Re Ga Ma′ Pa + Ga Ma′ – GaMa′ Pa, Ga Ma′ Dha Pa, Ṇi Re Ga – Re Re GaMa′ – GaMa′ Dha Pa, PaMa′ GaRe GaMa′ Pa, Pa Re Ga + Ga Re Ṇi Re Sa|
(3) Ga Ma′ Dha Ni – Ni Dha Pa + Ga Ma′ GaMa′ Ni Dha Pa, Ṇi Re – Re Ga – Ga Ma′ Ni Dha – Pa, Pa Ma′ – Re Ma′ Ga + Ga Re Ṇi Re Sa|

Thus it is clear that if, in the group of notes of a nyāsa (resting note), some special feature is shown and it is then given the form of a nyāsa again, that is called vinyāsa (phrase-ending note). Just as there is one sanyāsa (ending note of the first phrase) after many nyāsas, so in the same way there are many vinyāsas in one nyāsa; though they are uttered after the nyāsa, they are regarded as parts of the nyāsa. And apanyāsas (intermediate resting notes) occur anywhere in the middle of any nyāsa. This is the form of ālāpa (slow unmetred elaboration).
The wise call the span from a fixed note up to the fourth note a svasthāna. In the lower, middle and upper registers, four svasthānas are arranged.
blocks.verse:
अचला च्चतूर्थ पर्यन्तम् स्वस्थानम् कथ्यते बुधैः।
मन्द्र मध्यक तारेषु चतुः स्वस्थान योजना।१२१।

blocks.text: The group of notes from a fixed note (acal svara), that is Sa or 'Pa', up to the fourth note is called svasthāna (group from a fixed note up to the fourth). Just as a chariot is understood to be complete with four wheels, an animal or a cot with four legs, and a building with four directions, so four notes are needed for the ālāpa to dwell in. The remaining notes are for its development. That is why, in everyday speech, the word sargam (solfège) [Sa Re Ga Ma] is used so much.

Thus in practice there are four svasthānas across the three registers (saptaka), because the lower register (mandra saptaka) and the upper register (tāra saptaka) are not used in full; only half of each is used. So from Ma or Pa of the lower register up to Sa of the middle register is taken as the first svasthāna; then from middle Sa up to the note Ma the second svasthāna; then from middle Pa up to upper Ṡa the third svasthāna; and from upper Ṡa up to upper Ṁa the fourth svasthāna. In the svara vistāra (elaboration of notes) of any rāga these svasthānas are used in order. But in rāgas whose emphasis lies in the upper register, we cannot follow the order of the svasthānas when elaborating their notes; even so, the svasthāna has to be taken as the basis.

On the basis of the rules above, we are now going to present the svara vistāra (elaboration of notes) of a few rāgas. Rāgas are elaborated still further on the basis of the elements of tāna (tāna tattva). But here I do not wish to elaborate too much. The sādhaka (practitioner) should practise these elaborations sitting in the shade of the guru (teacher), and should sometimes use his own intelligence as well.
Doubt born of ignorance is a disease, and its medicine lies in the śāstra. Taking refuge in the guru as physician, one becomes content and attains peace.
blocks.verse:
अज्ञानात् संशयो व्याधिः शास्त्रे तस्यौषधिः स्थिता।
गुरूम् वैध्यम् समाश्रित्य सन्तुष्टः शान्तिमाप्नुयात्।१२२।

blocks.text: That is, because of ignorance many kinds of doubt arise in the mind. Doubt makes the mind sick. The medicine for this disease of doubt certainly lies in the śāstra (systematic treatise), but only by taking refuge in the physician who is the guru (teacher) can that doubt be removed. When doubt is removed, the mind attains peace.

A note in a circle is the vādī (principal note); one in a half circle is the saṃvādī (consonant second note); one within two halves is the vivādī (dissonant note); and the unmarked notes are the anuvādī (assonant notes).
blocks.verse:
गोला कारे तु वादी स्यात् संवादी त्वर्ध गोलके।
अर्धद्वये विवादीस्या न्निश्चिन्हास्त्वनुवादिनः।१२३।

blocks.text: Two notes joined by a staff-shaped sign (daṇḍākāra) are meant to go together (saṅgati, companionship of notes). Notes here with the snake sign (sarpa cihna) are always to be oscillated (kampita).
blocks.verse:
दण्डा कारेण संबद्धौ स्वरौ संगतये मतौ।
सर्प चिन्हाः स्वराः ह्यत्र भवेयुः कम्पिताः सदा।१२४।

blocks.text: The signs for tīvra and the other [altered] notes were made long ago by Nārāyaṇa [Bhātkhaṇḍe ji]. The wise should learn them by seeing them in the ascent and the descent.
blocks.verse:
तीव्रादीनां तु संकेतः कृतो नारायणैः पुरा।
दृष्ट्वारोहेऽवरोहे च ज्ञातव्यास्ते मनीषिभि।१२५।

blocks.text: In the ślokas above, some symbolic signs for the notes have been given. On the basis of these signs we shall get a general introduction to rāgas through their āroha avaroha (ascent and descent) alone. For a detailed introduction, other śāstras (treatises) of music may be consulted.
(1) Take the note written inside a circle as the vādī (principal note), e.g. - [Ga]
(2) Notes written in a half circle are to be regarded as saṃvādī (consonant second note), e.g. - °Ni
(3) Take notes placed within two half circles as vivādī (dissonant note), e.g. - °Ma°
(4) Where in the ascent we mark Ga Ma Pa Dha in this form, the companionship (saṅgati) of those two notes will be rāga-identifying.
(5) Take the notes that have a snake-like sign beneath them as oscillated (āndolita) in that rāga, e.g. Ga
Apart from these, the signs for tīvra and other notes will be taken from the works of the late Śrī Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇ Bhātkhaṇḍe ji, which were settled long ago.

Here the book has not been lengthened by giving the svara vistāra (elaboration of notes) of more rāgas, but the scientific basis of the method of ālāpa (svara vistāra) has been made clear. From the elaborations above it has become clear to us that the sign of nyāsa (resting note) and vinyāsa (phrase-ending note) can be used in the nyāsa, and the sign (mark) of vinyāsa in the vinyāsa. In other books nyāsa and vinyāsa have one and the same sign, e.g. - ṆiReGa, Ni Ma′ Re Ga, Re Ga Re Ma′ Ga and so on. But for apanyāsa (intermediate resting note) a sign of broken shape (khaṇḍākāra) has been given, e.g. - Ni Re Ga Ma′ Pa – Pa Ma′ Ga, Ga Ma′ Dha Pa – Re Ga and so on. For sanyāsa (ending note of the first phrase) all treatises give the sign of the full stop. So if, by the method described earlier, we understand the separate importance of the notes of rāgas and do the svara vistāra ourselves, and keep testing whether it is right or wrong by looking at the svara vistāras given in other books, it is possible that our sādhanā (practice) will succeed.
From svarālāpa comes layālāpa, and from that the mukta tāna; joining these into songs and the like, one should practise them with the tāla.
blocks.verse:
स्वरालापाल्लयालापो मुक्तान स्ततो भवेत्।
गीतादिषु समायुज्य तान्स्तालेन समभ्यसेत्।१२६।

blocks.text: Just as a bale of cotton is spread out and opened up, then given the form of thread and then made into cloth, after which the cloth is cut, sewn and so on according to one's various needs, and only then becomes fit for use - raw cotton by itself is used in only a few places - in the same way the ārohāvaroha (ascent and descent) form of a rāga is elaborated by the method of nyāsa and the rest, and then laya (tempo) is brought into that svara vistāra (elaboration of notes); this is called layālāpa (ālāpa in rhythm) or joḍ-ālāpa. Then, from it, on the basis of layakārī (rhythmic play) and the elements of tāna (tāna tattva), thread in the form of tānas is made. After that we are able to use them within a fixed tāla (metric cycle), together with tihāīs and so on. This is the meaning of the śloka above. As an example, three things are being presented in one rāga.
